name: Trusting God in trouble
about: Affliction, comfort, and waiting on the Lord.

teachings.title: Counted as sheep for the slaughter
teachings.summary: The lament of Psalm 44 is turned into instruction in Romans 8 that nothing can separate us from Christ's love, and believers grown weak by comfort must be prepared to endure persecution, even the coming tribulation, without losing faith.
teachings.text:
**1 Peter 4:12–14**
*Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you: But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ’s sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy. If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified.*

If the people who call themselves by His name we're naturally like Stephen, standing up for the faith and being willing to suffer death for the truth while forgiving those that stoned him to death, the New Testament wouldn't be so full of warnings and encouragement.

In **Psalm 44:22–24** they cry out desperately to God;
*Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter. Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever. Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and forgettest our affliction and our oppression?*

The same lament is turned to edifying instruction in the New Testament;

**Romans 8:35–37**
*Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.*

Because man is naturally going to complain in the best of times, we need to be prepared for the proper attitude in the worst. To be persuaded that nothing can separate us from the love of Christ. Even when things are bleak.

Jesus Himself gave this encouragement to the church in Smyrna, who were facing real persecution at the hands of their enemies.

**Revelation 2:8–11**
*And unto the angel of the church in Smyrna write; These things saith the first and the last, which was dead, and is alive; I know thy works, and tribulation, and poverty, (but thou art rich) and I know the blasphemy of them which say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.*

Just as the instructions to live separated lives, to be holy as He is holy, is necessary because man does not by his fleshly nature do good works, even those who are saved, the same flesh tends to need reminders of past victory, while still may cry out "Why?" to their Saviour.

Righteous Job did. The best man of his generation, and yet he sought answers from God, and sinned not with his mouth while doing so, according to scripture.

Modern American Christians, made weak by the comforts and bounty God has graciously given our nation, grown fat off His blessings, will most assuredly cry out the same laments when the abomination of desolation is rolled out, and the armies of the beast strike us down.

Even the spirits of the martyrs in Great Tribulation will cry out, impatiently.

**Revelation 6:9–10**
*And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?*

We naturally may feel abandoned in the thick of it. Crying out, as the congregation does, is sadly expected.

*Awake, why sleepest thou, O Lord? arise, cast us not off for ever. Wherefore hidest thou thy face, and forgettest our affliction and our oppression?*

We may be beaten down, bowed to the dust, despondent.

teachings.title: Counted as sheep for the slaughter, yet faithful
teachings.summary: Psalm 44 shows the faithful, who cannot apostatize, can suffer without being punished for sin, and Paul uses it to show God eventually delivers His people.
teachings.text:
What makes **Psalm 44** so jarring and often makes modern readers uncomfortable, is that the congregation is stating they are not being punished for apostasy or adultery or for being unfaithful.

In many other laments, Israel confesses their sins and acknowledges that their defeat is a righteous judgment from God. But here, they boldly declare their innocence:

*All this is come upon us; yet have we not forgotten thee, neither have we dealt falsely in thy covenant... If we have forgotten the name of our God... Shall not God search this out?*

Travails come upon the just. Upon the faithful who have placed their trust in the Lord.

The psalmists raise a relevant point today; believers may cry out to God and ask why they are suffering, knowing they have not fallen to apostasy.

These sons of Korah are believers, and believers cannot apostatize. They feel confident in asking God to search their hearts for any sign of adultery in worship of Him.

They may, amongst themselves, talk about how the northern kingdom of Israel which was also being afflicted in this time by the Assyrian empire, deserved it. They had fallen into the sin of Jeroboam and gone after strange gods.

But these faithful Levites could wonder what they themselves may have done to bring upon these attacks.

Whatever other sins they may have had in their lives or collectively, they still were faithful to the Lord.

They did exactly what Deuteronomy 6 commanded. They listened to their fathers. They trusted not in their own bows or swords. They kept the faith, yet they were still *scattered among the heathen* and *counted as sheep for the slaughter*, and yet still faced tribulation.

Paul quotes **Psalm 44** in **Romans** for exactly this reason. To show that God eventually does deliver the faithful. That we can count on him even when it seems like the entire world is against us.

Paul is using the same technique of teaching to the children the stories of the fathers, to bring us hope. Judah was delivered from the Assyrians. And the faithful were delivered by the promise of Christ being fulfilled.

Using then a past lament to give future hope, and show the strength of God in keeping His promises is the entire point of the commandment.

We see the Deliverance of God's people into the promised land in the past used as hope for the people then present Jerusalem, and their cries are then given to us as hope today knowing that they were eventually delivered.

If we are scattered to the wilderness, to the place of dragons, or are led through the valley of the shadow of death, we have that hope within us. The call to have the patience of Job. The faith of the fathers. The understanding of Paul.

So stand fast and comfort one another with these words.

teachings.title: Hope thou in God
teachings.summary: In the spiritual siege believers face from a hostile world, God promises to draw nigh to those who turn to Him in humility, so we can hope in Him and praise Him with confidence.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 43** is a shorter song of the same theme as **Psalm 42,** a condensed appeal to the Lord in desperate times.

The call to judge, that is to be a deliverer, an advocate, to bring the cause of the prayerful against the ungodly that afflict them, is the heart of it.

We may not be in the straits of captivity or war, or even persecution by our own government for the cause of Christ, and praise God for sparing us, but modern American Christians can find ourselves in calamity and a spiritual siege.

**Ephesians 6:12**
*For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.*

We may face opposition by the ungodly in our families, workplace, neighborhoods, even in some churches, anywhere that we find our faith and longsuffering tested by the slings and arrows of those who hate us and our Lord. Jesus warned us.

**John 15:18**
*If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.*

He warned us that He would bring division, even among family.

**Luke 12:51–53**
*Suppose ye that I am come to give peace on earth? I tell you, Nay; but rather division: For from henceforth there shall be five in one house divided, three against two, and two against three. The father shall be divided against the son, and the son against the father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against the mother; the mother in law against her daughter in law, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.*

In any of this, the lack of scale and immediate physical danger doesn't change the fact that our heart can grow despondent over our circumstances, and the spiritual battles can be as consequential as the real world wars, at times.

Reminding ourselves that Jesus is the God of our strength, the Rock of our salvation, even when we feel far from Him, is a common prayer in these Psalms, and with good reason.

In **Zechariah 1:3**, the Bible says *Turn ye unto me, saith the Lord of hosts, and I will turn unto you*. A promise of God, repeated in the Epistles;

**James 4:7–8**
*Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.*

The reminder to come to God in humble confession is key, but the overall concept that God seeks our repentance **towards** Him, that He will close the gap and draw nigh is a fundamental doctrine, and a hope we see promised and delivered time and again in scripture.

And in our peril, and in our desperate need, if we turn to God and humble ourselves before Him, and ask for His judgement, He will come to us and lift us up in His arms, and lead us to where we need to be.

By His wonderful light and truth, we know the way to Him. Jesus said He is the way, the truth and the life, the light of the world, guiding us to His holy hill, the tents of His people, the mansions of glory.

By the gospel shared among the people, the desperate are led to the house of God. To the local church, where His praises are sung in our deliverance, and where mourning may turn to joy.

*Then will I go unto the altar of God, unto God my exceeding joy: yea, upon the harp will I praise thee, O God my God.*

The definitive *Then will I go*, shows the confidence in His promise. But the doubts of the flesh can cause us to be cast down. Depressed at the situation and wondering when God's hand will lift us up. The psalmist reconciles these two things in the person's spirit, this contradiction between the heart and the spirit, with the encouragement to hope in God.

To know *Then will I go* because He is faithful and true. That no matter what comes, we shall praise Him. Here in the congregation, or in the heavenly choir. He is our God. Amen

teachings.title: Hope thou in God: the poor in spirit lifted up
teachings.summary: Psalm 43, rightly kept separate in the KJV, shifts from lament to certain hope, showing God lifts up the poor in spirit, not only the super-faithful.
teachings.text:
**Psalms 42 and 43** share the refrain;

*Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.*

And there are no attributions given to **Psalm 43** in the Hebrew, the way **Psalm 42** is attributed to the "sons of Korah."

Some translations and traditions combine the two songs, to make it one continuous Psalm.

While no one can say with any certainty, I believe the KJV translators were wise and Spirit guided to keep them separated. While the themes are similar as far as the broken-hearted nature of them, and the repeated refrain, they each carry a weight and purpose unique to themselves.

The longer appeal in **Psalm 42** is more of a meditation on the despondency of man in these circumstances, while the more brief and succinct **Psalm 43** tips the balance more to the understanding of God's promises and the faith that overcomes the fear.

Yes we still find the lament of our diminished spirit, but the focus has shifted slightly to the certain hope.

It's brief nature makes it a more accessible devotional and gives someone who is coming out of depression a more focused resolution.

But, taken together the last several Psalms show that the poor of spirit are exactly who God seeks to lift up. That His promises aren't only for the super-faithful warriors, but the meek and lowly.

It is good to have a God Who understands our infirmities, and His Word as a relatable resource in our time of need.

teachings.title: As the hart panteth after the water brooks
teachings.summary: Even mature believers can be downcast and mocked in trials, but troubles strengthen faith, and the hope of the living water in Christ never leaves us ashamed.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 42** is a gut-punch of a song, a prayer of desperation from a troubled believer, being strengthened in their faith, while simultaneously going through the wringer.

The psalmists (this psalm is attributed to the "Sons of Korah," likely the musicians and singers in the Temple) write of a man whose soul is panting after the Lord, as a hart, or deer, pants after the water of a brook. The thirst of need.

*My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?*

A plaintive lament, needing the Lord so badly that we'd like to die, just to be with Him and at peace. *Tears have been my meat,* the psalmist says. All he has consumed, day and night, while scoffers say, *Where is thy God?*

The spiritual thirst, though tears have fed him, is a powerful metaphor. But we have the promise of living waters, in which we shall never thirst. The promise that our spirit will be quenched in Christ.

**John 4:14**
*But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life.*

This promise is true and we can count on it, but the trials of this life can leave us panting for the living water, to be satisfied by them in the thirst we develop during low points in our lives.

The psalmist writes of the remembrance of his joy in the Lord, the times he sang and worshipped in the congregation during holidays, and asks himself why is he so down and depressed. He knows he will yet praise God, when He turns His face towards him.

Knowing that in the past, he's been delivered and trusting it will happen again, isn't just a comfort but in a way, a condemnation against himself.

"Why am I so down hearted in my soul, when I can remember and appreciate all God has done for me, and my faith that he will again?" This is a place that even a mature Christian can come to. It is the truth that the weariness of this life can beat us down, even with unshakable faith.

As Pastor Jack Hyles often preached, you can't have unshakable faith unless your faith has been shaken.

The troubles become the source for the strength of our conviction. Because in trouble we are shown His power.

And in our darkest moments, the voices of the scoffers cut like a knife. Satan uses them to attack our faith, as he sought to shake Job's.

**Job 1:8–11**
*And the LORD said unto Satan, Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a perfect and an upright man, one that feareth God, and escheweth evil? Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought? Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face.*

The mocking of the unrighteous, who delight to see God's children stumble, to say "Aha" when we fall, stems from this same desire Satan has, when he accused the brethren day and night before the Lord. Seeking whom he may devour.

But we have the peace of God in tribulation, even if we are despondent in the moment, we know He is true.

**Romans 5:1–6**
*Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.*

We were delivered from death into new life, at our worst. The hope we have in Christ will never leave us ashamed. Let them laugh us to scorn, we shall be saved and the Lord will cast them down.

teachings.title: Why art thou cast down, O my soul
teachings.summary: Remembering past deliverance does not automatically cure depression; it is fine to ask God why, without beating ourselves up, as long as we do not forget Him.
teachings.text:
*Why art thou cast down, O my soul?* It is a comfort to any believer to realize that remembering past deliverances doesn't automatically cure present depression.

We may take the moment of our pain and beat ourselves up for not appreciating what God has done for us. For allowing sadness and heartache to linger. Or that sorrow to affect us in ways that makes everything worse, when our own memories of past deliverance aren't enough to make us snap out of it, and we question and blame ourselves.

True conviction is forged precisely when the storms are howling. Faith isn't the absence of trouble; it is the stubborn decision to anchor oneself to the Rock when you feel like you are drowning.

Every life has seasons of strife. We shouldn't wallow in self-pity, but we can recognize our need for working through grief without beating ourselves up for it.

We know the truth of Christ. We will sing His praise again. This too shall pass. But in the moment, it's okay to *say unto God my rock, Why hast thou forgotten me?* Just don't take this feeling as an excuse to forget God.

teachings.title: A friend that sticketh closer than a brother
teachings.summary: When friends and even family betray us at our lowest, as Judas betrayed Christ in fulfilment of Psalm 41, Jesus understands and will never leave nor forsake us.
teachings.text:
During his low point of illness and enemies scheming, David mentions betrayal.

*Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.*

The truth is that we often face betrayal at the most inopportune times, when we are at our lowest. Or even those we trusted and rely on, letting us down when we need them the most.

This truth is one of the most devastating things we grapple with in life. Not that there are bad people who seek our harm, but there are close friends, even brothers, who turn on us in our darkest hours.

*But thou, O LORD, be merciful unto me, and raise me up, that I may requite them.*

Jesus explicitly quotes **Psalm 41:9** during the Last Supper in **John 13:18**;
*He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.*

David’s specific pain was a literal prophecy of Christ’s betrayal by Judas. Jesus knows our infirmities, He has suffered our pains. He knows what it is like to be betrayed by those closest to Him. (Not only the evil of Judas, but also being denied by Peter, who loves Him)

But, thanks be to God that He is steadfast and true. The Lord raises us up, and gives us the strength to overcome their evil, that it all turn out good, because He loves us.

**Proverbs 18:24**
*A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother*.

That friend is Jesus Christ.

Even our family may turn against us.

**Matthew 10:34-36**
*Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword. For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law. And a man’s foes shall be they of his own household.*

But we have the assurance and knowledge that He will always be there for us. *For he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee*.

**Deuteronomy 31:6**
*Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the Lord thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.*

We can take comfort in Jesus' own promise to us:…*and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.*

Amen.

teachings.title: Many are the afflictions of the righteous
teachings.summary: God's commandments are for our good and He provides for His own, yet the godly will suffer affliction that grows faith, and none who trust Him will be desolate.
teachings.text:
Those that trust in the Lord know they shall never want. We are protected from evil by a host of angels. We are given our daily bread.

**Psalms 37:25**
*I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread*.

We may not be rich, we may not be feasting on expensive meals. But the Lord will provide for his own.

And the Lord promises us that we shall have a long life with good in it if we keep ourselves from speaking lies and doing evil, and rather seek peace and pursue it. Loving our neighbors.

While the Commandments of the Lord serve to let us know that we have fallen short of His perfect ways, they are given that it be well with us. That if we follow them, we have an easier life full of blessings. They are for our benefit, not to oppress us.

We are judged by the law of Liberty, not saved by our works. But our works can benefit us in our service to God.

God's eyes are upon us and he listens for our prayers, when we walk in the truth. And he is against those who commit evil, and he chastens every son He receives.

*Many are the afflictions of the righteous: but the LORD delivereth him out of them all.*

**2 Timothy 3:12**
*Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution*.

While we are promised a longer life with more blessings, we are not promised a carefree life that has no suffering. Often the suffering we experience is for our benefit to help us grow in the Lord, and to increase our faith.

Praise and obedience and calling upon the Lord, and the tribulations that we suffer, all work together for good. Because they increase our faith.

The LORD redeemeth the soul of his servants: and none of them that trust in him shall be desolate.

This is the promise given to all believers. That once we are saved we are always saved.b that we shall never be left desolate. Will never be ashamed for our trust in the Lord.

He will redeem The souls of his servants and bring us out of tribulation and into Glory, in His holy name. Amen

teachings.title: In the midst of the congregation will I praise thee
teachings.summary: Trials are an opportunity to overcome by God's power and praise Him among the brethren, which cannot be done by forsaking the assembly.
teachings.text:
Psalm 22 continues. The desperate plea of the condemned man, compassed by dogs, scorned and ridiculed, pierced and heartbroken, feeling abandoned by God, turns to a prayer of certain hope.

We know God has delivered every promise He has made. He has heard the cries of His people and, in due season, saved them.

We may persist in our prayers, reminding God, and ourselves, of His faithfulness, as we ask for more immediate relief. His perfect timing may not be ours, but at our weakest He shows His strength.

*Deliver my soul from the sword; my darling from the power of the dog. Save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.*

From the proverbial horns of a dilemma, from the immediate threat, we call upon the name of the Lord. Not only the saved, His darling, but the lost often find His strength in their time of trial. Foxhole converts.

The Potter often moves the clay in such a way, that we finally see our shortcomings and impotency, and need His hand to lift us up, that we may be what He has planned for us to become.

If even Jesus Christ was to be made a reproach and murdered by bloody men in a wicked act, that we may know eternal life, as the risen and triumphant Son of God, then our trials are an opportunity to overcome by His power and to give the Lord the glory.

*I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee.*

In the midst of tribulation, we shall praise Him. That is the mind of a mature Christian. It is difficult to see, sometimes, and we may feel isolated, alone, but in our most desperate hour, we praise Him. We declare His holy name to our brethren, in the congregation we hold up His excellence.

(It may not be a primary (or even secondary) application of this psalm, but it strikes me that we cannot lift up our voice in praise to the congregation, to declare His name unto the brethren, if we avoid church. If we forsake the assembly. Go to church!)

teachings.title: Afflicted for doing the work of God
teachings.summary: Believers who serve God, like a sister just after winning a soul, will be attacked, and should patiently endure so their faith grows and their light shines.
teachings.text:
There are so many problems we will have in our life, as men on the earth, and persecutions and attacks added on top of them for believers, if we do the works of God. If we serve Him, we will see trouble.

How often do we experience or witness the attacks of the devil on believers who turn to God, and do His work?

I was talking with a younger sister in Christ who just won someone to the Lord, and how awesome that was. Within a few days, she was being afflicted from all sides by multiple travails and trials.

It was good to be able to give her this perspective. To know to patiently endure it, and see her faith grow. To turn to trusting the Lord to see her through it, and to love on those around her so that they will see her light so shine, that they'll praise God in Heaven. That the unsaved might be persuaded by her chaste conversation. Her behavior in the face of adversity.

David's story is a wonderful example of how we should view things. His Psalms help sharpen that focus on God when we are really going through it.

We can humbly ask God for His mercy, and know that He who has lifted us up from the gates of death will save us, while the heathen and enemies of God will be snared by their own sin and turned into Hell. Amen

teachings.title: Brought back by tribulation, still sick of love
teachings.summary: The backslidden believer may be brought back through persecution and tribulation, yet like the bride she will not renounce her beloved.
teachings.text:
This could be false teachers, those religious leaders who were not able to give her the gospel, now kicking her when she's down, to try and spoil her faith.

We may backslide. We may become complacent. We may try to avoid doing His work. We may ignore His calling and then, when tribulation comes, look for Him where He is not, seeking answers. And we may be subject to tribulation, to remind us that we need Him, to remind us we are His.

Just as Jonah was brought to Nineveh in the whale. Just as the church in Jerusalem, ordained to spread the gospel to the four corners of the world, stayed in Judea until the persecution against them scattered many. Just like Paul's repeated attempts to win his countrymen led him again and again to Jerusalem, finally being brought out and delivered to Rome in chains.

It's hard to kick against the pricks.

And so beaten and bloody, the bride charges an oath to the daughters of Jerusalem; *if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.*

To our modern years this sounds bad, but what's being said is that she is sick from love, overwhelmed by her feelings. Lovesick for her beloved.

Despite persecution, she will not renounce him. Despite tribulation for his sake, she still longs for him. And she tells others who may be seeking him to give him her message of love.

teachings.title: Whom the Lord loveth he correcteth
teachings.summary: God's chastening when we stray is a mark that we are sons and should be received with thanks, and Wisdom, by which God founded the earth, is Jesus Himself, the way and the tree of life.
teachings.text:
*My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.*

Gaining wisdom and understanding comes also from His chastening when we don't keep to His paths, when we stray to our own understanding. Like a mule that may wander off the path is whipped, so too are we chastened. And we should be thankful.

**Hebrews 12:7-8** *ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons; for what son is he whom the father chasteneth not? But if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons.*

Be happy in chastening. Delight in His law. Gain understanding, covet Wisdom the way men covet riches, because it is more precious than silver, gold or rubies or any of the merchandise of the world.

Wealth cannot extend your life and give you health, not like the Lord can. And love of money is the root of all evil, and for covetousness sake come wars. But pursuing Wisdom brings life.

*Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and honour.*

Her paths lead to peace. Wisdom is a tree of life! So by faith we step out on the paths, and keep the commandments, understanding the promises of God.

The Lord by wisdom hath founded the earth. Creation is by His knowledge and understanding. And knowing all things were created by His Word, through Christ Jesus, we see that Jesus IS the way, the truth, the light that is described throughout Proverbs. He is Wisdom. He is the tree of life. We are followers of the Way. We follow Jesus.

teachings.title: Like Job, our end better than our beginning
teachings.summary: Like Job, believers pass through trials from the Accuser, but by grace through faith our end at the adoption and resurrection will be glorious, joint heirs with Christ.
teachings.text:
A reflection on **Job** and his later end being better than his first, and the salvation of his (and our) Redeemer:

Like Job, we are born of woman and blessed by God to an abundant life, no matter our station, having life. When temptation comes, and the law enters, and sin slays us, the Accuser, Satan, does his worst to us (tempered by God's mercy).

We have trials, and tribulations. But, entering into grace by faith, we have the hope and promise of God in Christ that our end will be better than our beginning. That at the adoption, when we put on immortality and shed corruption, when we are redeemed, our end will be glorious, as we will be like Him. And like Lot's children, male or female, we are made joint heirs with Christ.

teachings.title: Our later end greater than our former
teachings.summary: Our trials are an opportunity to know God better and grow in faith, because in Christ our bondage is turned to liberty and our later end will be greater than the beginning.
teachings.text:
The Lord gave Job a long life, to see four generations come from these children. And so Job died, being old and full of days. Quite a ways away from his lamenting his own birth.

Our struggles and temptations may never be as horrific and total as Job's test. We may seek to know why from the Lord. We may be tempted to blame Him, to curse God and die, as Job's wife said. Others may use the occasion to imply we deserve it.

But we should see the opportunity to better know God. To grow our faith, and our understanding of Him. To know that here, or in the resurrection, we shall overcome.

The Lord will deliver us, He has turned the captivity, the bondage of sin we are all under, to liberty in Christ. We have the Comforter sent by Him. Our later end will always be greater than our former, because we are all heirs in Jesus.

*But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.*

Amen.

teachings.title: Suffering defies neat explanations
teachings.summary: Though God can use suffering to correct, Job's affliction was not for his sin, so the wise response to another's grief is humble presence and charity, not overconfident correction.
teachings.text:
Elihu's point about God speaking through dreams and visions or through pain and affliction to turn people from pride and the pit isn't entirely wrong theologically (Scripture elsewhere affirms God can use suffering redemptively **Psalm 119:67, 71; Hebrews 12:5–11).** But applying it directly to Job's case assumes the suffering is for specific sin or pride, which the book's prologue shows isn't the full story. Job's trials stem from a heavenly challenge, not personal wrongdoing. But Elihu's unable to hold enough grace and empathy to relate to Job in charity. In faith.

Young (or any) believers gain influence through quiet godliness, love, and purity, not puffed-up words that lack empathy for profound grief. Job's story shows that suffering often defies neat explanations, and the wisest response is often humble presence rather than overconfident correction.

Everyone else's misfortune isn't an opportunity to show how smart or wise or spiritual you are. No one profits from that. It leads to men despising your youth, not establishing you as more wise than they are

teachings.title: Retribution theology is man's, not God's
teachings.summary: Job's friends argue that suffering proves sin, but God's verdict on them shows this karma theology is human, not His.
teachings.text:
Job 4 will begin a dialogue between Job and the three friends who came to him to mourn.

The first to reply to Job's plaintive cry, cursing the day he was born, is Eliphaz the Temanite, of Teman, a city in Edom. (**Genesis 36:11, 15; Jeremiah 49:7, 20; Ezekiel 25:13**). His initial argument is made in chapters 4 and 5, and offers a view of "retribution theology," the idea of karma in God's doings. That sin is the cause of suffering, and that you get what you deserve.

Job’s friends defend retribution theology rigorously, and it is difficult to disagree with many of the points made, from a human perspective. Much of it sounds right in our minds. So, before we dive deeper into the text, we should keep in mind the end of the matter, where (spoilers), God addresses the men and what they say.

**Job 42:7-9**
*And it was so, that after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, the Lord said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath. Therefore take unto you now seven bullocks and seven rams, and go to my servant Job, and offer up for yourselves a burnt offering; and my servant Job shall pray for you: for him will I accept: lest I deal with you after your folly, in that ye have not spoken of me the thing which is right, like my servant Job. So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went, and did according as the Lord commanded them: the Lord also accepted Job.*

The friends of Job, (and later, the young accuser Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite), are given opportunity to make multiple philosophical and theological points regarding the nature of God, His justice and their natural suspicion of those who suffer as being sinners, and worse, that those that suffer worse than they do must be greater sinners than they are.

This line of thought is just as common today as it was then, and is human nature. But not God's. And while there is general wisdom to be found in their arguments, the application they choose to make is wrong.

As we go, it is good to keep this in mind, especially when we read something that seems perfectly reasonable to us, and may reflect our own views that we may have held against others in our life. It should cause self-reflection.

teachings.title: Shall we not receive evil? His grace is sufficient
teachings.summary: Job's patience and Paul's thorn teach that our suffering serves to glorify God's grace and humble us, for His strength is made perfect in weakness.
teachings.text:
The Book of Job continues into chapter 2. I've often thought that, had Job been confined to just the first chapter it would serve as a great lesson in patience and understanding in the faith. But in the wisdom of God it continues, bringing many other lessons to us.

Again, the spirits of the righteous men in Heaven come before God, and among them the devil comes. And again he's been to and fro in the Earth, and walking up and down it.

And the Lord said unto Satan hast thou considered Job? That there's none like him the perfect and upright man, who is still holding fast his integrity even though Satan had moved God to destroy him without a cause.

And Satan says that a man will give up anything for his life. He calls God to afflict Job by touching his bone in flesh and says that he will curse God to His face. And so God agrees, saying only take not his life. And Satan afflicts Job with postulant boils from The souls of his feet to the crown of his head.

Poor Job sits in ash, mourning, And now is taking a shard of pottery to his skin to scrape himself of the sores. Miserable, having lost everything and now afflicted with a painful and disgusting curse.

His wife is disgusted with his continued faith, and says curse God and die. But he said that this is foolish. That if we receive good at the hands of God shall we not receive evil?

And Job sinned not with his lips.

The continued patience of Job is a testament that we should seek to emulate. As bad as things are we've all been blessed beyond anything we deserve by God's grace. His grace is sufficient.

Paul, similarly had bemoaned a thorn in his flesh, appealing to God three times saying that he would be so much more useful in the cause of Christ if he had it removed. It took him a while to understand.

**2 Corinthians 12:6-9**
*For though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth: but now I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me to be, or that he heareth of me. And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.*

Our suffering exists for many reasons, but ultimately it is to give glory to God for His grace and His mercy. That while we are weak He is strong and our strength. Even if it's just to humble us that we glory not in ourselves.

And so the scene shifts as three of Job's friends arrive from far off, barely recognizing him. They enter and sit down with him on the ground, for 7 days and seven nights and none speak to him for they saw that his grief was very great.

We will learn more about each as the story progresses.

teachings.title: Job and the hedge of protection
teachings.summary: Job shows that both wealth and affliction are to God's glory, refuting both the idea that only the wicked prosper and the prosperity gospel, while Satan, the god of this world, works only within what God allows.
teachings.text:
Now God knows who Satan is and what he does and His pointing out Job is deliberate, and in so many ways this is done for our admonition, upon whom the end of the world has come.

If a man as upright and perfect in his ways can be sorely tempted by the persecution of Satan against him, If the hedge of protection may be lifted, to show the glory of God for such a man as job, how can we expect the small tragedies that befall us as believers to be any less to His glory?

If the Book of Job was one chapter, the lesson is present and clear. But as we'll see, there is so many more lessons to learn than simple perseverance in faith.

Satan of course credits the hedge of protection God has placed around Job and his family and the blessings of the holdings that he's acquired which are gifts of God, as the only reason Job's faith is so strong. He says to God that if He put forth His hand now and touched all that he had, Job would curse Him to his face.

I have seen an error among people similar to this, that says only the wicked prosper. Job shows this isn't the case and that wealth in itself is not a bad thing, but that all we have is a gift of God.

Then there's the prosperity Gospel types, who falsely say that if you're not successful and you're not succeeding, that you're not right with God.

But here we humbly learn that whether we are blessed or cursed, all is to His glory. As Paul writes:

**Philippians 4:12**
*I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need*.

Whether you're in good times or bad times or the mix most of us find ourselves in, it's all to the glory of God. His grace is sufficient.

Now the Lord says to Satan, *behold all that he hath is in thy power* but bars him from doing harm to Job physically.

The prime interpretation of this is that God has granted Satan special permission to afflict Job, And that is a fair reading of the text, especially in light of the hedge of protection Satan says God has placed about Job. But, as I've mentioned, the Bible says that Satan is the god of this world, That he is the prince of the power of the air, ruler of this world. Not as God, but as having influence and power over the things of this Earth.

So is the Lord reminding Satan, or enabling him? It's difficult to say. But we should keep it in mind always.

**Ephesians 6:12**
*For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.*

But regardless, Satan is given the power to affect all that Job has, if not his person. And in one day, he does his worst.

First we see that his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine and in the eldest brother's house, this detail is given before the rest, creating tension in the reader.

Then the messengers begin to arrive. One tells of the oxen and asses killed by marauding Sabeans, who are from the south, where modern Yemen is.

Then another arrives to say that the fire of God reigned from Heaven on the sheep in the servants and consumed them.

When God gave permission to Satan to do what he will, he gave him access to the fire of God that rains from Heaven.

**Revelation 13:11-13**
*And I beheld another beast coming up out of the earth; and he had two horns like a lamb, and he spake as a dragon. And he exerciseth all the power of the first beast before him, and causeth the earth and them which dwell therein to worship the first beast, whose deadly wound was healed. And he doeth great wonders, so that he maketh fire come down from heaven on the earth in the sight of men*

The false prophet of the Antichrist will have this power and ability, And it will cause the unsaved to worship the beast and his image.

teachings.title: Why God left the Canaanites in the land
teachings.summary: God left the heathen in the land to test Israel, and tribulation and evil today likewise test us and humble men to call on Christ.
teachings.text:
The pattern of falling away, turning to God for deliverance, and God sending a judge to free the children of Israel begins.

We see that God determines that the heathen in the land that they had failed to utterly remove will serve as a means to test the people, to keep them ready for war, to humble them, to tempt them to marry their outlandish woman and worship their false gods.

And when they suffered the fruit of their adultery, and came to see their need for God's salvation, repented towards Him, and called upon His name, He would send a deliverer.

In the same way, tribulation and sin in the world serve to test man, and as a schoolmaster, bring people to be humbled before God and seek His help. To call upon the name of Christ, the judge of all, to deliver us.

The Jews, who say they are but are not and do lie, exist in this world for the same reason these Canaanites do. The same with every evil organization of men.

They are here to keep us spiritually equipped for war. To tempt us into sin and worship of false gods. To test us and try us. To bring us to Him.

You can almost hear an ancient Israelite saying "of God real, why bad things happen? Why Chushanrishathaim attack us?"

Here in Judges we see exactly why. And it is to glory God.

teachings.title: Hard times turn us to the Lord
teachings.summary: As Israel turned to God in hard times and fell away in good, God uses tribulation to prove us and work patience, experience and hope.
teachings.text:
But we see the pattern. The harder the times, the more likely the people turn to the Lord. The better the times, the quicker they fall away.

In our Christian life, we may see similar patterns. There's a tendency towards leaning on God, turning to prayer more often, reading the Bible more, increasing church attendance, maybe even fasting...but when the deliverance comes, many begin to shirk those things. And rather than walk in the Spirit, backslide towards walking in the flesh.

God uses tribulation to prove us. That we may learn to trust Him more, to increase our faith. To learn mercy and judgement. To increase patience.

We see it throughout the Epistles.

**Romans 5:1-5**
*Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.*

It's the same pattern, spiritual rather than physical, but similar. A picture of our Christian life.

teachings.title: Faith in the face of giants
teachings.summary: Like Caleb, faith acts on belief rather than fear, and God delivers through tribulation and builds our faith as we trust Him.
teachings.text:
**Numbers 13:30**
*And Caleb stilled the people before Moses, and said, Let us go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it.*

The faith of Caleb in the face of what seemed overwhelming odds, saved him while the fear of the other spies condemned them.

You cannot be delivered by God from tribulation, without tribulation. You cannot make manifest the glory of God without first being weak.

Faith is acting on belief rather than doubt, trusting on hope rather than fear.

From salvation, knowing first we are sinners deserving death and Hell, but trusting Christ to redeem us, and so calling upon the name of the Lord to save us, to allowing God to deliver us from evil by faith, rather than taking charge ourselves in fear and our own destruction, faith that He strengthens us, that even giants will be destroyed before us, is the means of obtaining the promised hope.

**Hebrews 11:1**
*Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.*

We believe something unseen to be true, and despite doubts we act on that faith by the unseen evidence we trust in our hearts, that we may receive that which we hope for. And God rewards us for it, building our faith.

As long as we walk in that Spirit of truth, faith continues to build, and the hopes we have are obtained.

teachings.title: We have no excuse
teachings.summary: Since we do not face death for preaching as the prophets did, we have no excuse not to serve, and should rejoice in tribulation.
teachings.text:
Be thankful for living when we do, in times where we aren't directly threatened with stocks, stripes or death for the preaching of the cross. We have no excuse.

We live in a time and place where, while we may see tribulation, where we may have the god of this world come against us if we strive for the Gospel, doing our Father's will. Winning souls. Edifying the brethren. We won't face death the way the prophets did. Praise God.

And so we have no excuse.

In fact, if you have done anything for the Lord, you may have already felt the attacks of Satan and his children on you. And yet, if you rejoice in the temptations and praise God for the tribulation that worketh patience in you, you will be delivered.

We have no excuse.

And if the times become more hostile, and persecution for the faith more common, still rejoice.

**Matthew 10:28**
*And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell*.

We will still have no excuse.

teachings.title: Jeremiah teaches us to face a nation's judgment
teachings.summary: Jeremiah and Lamentations prepare believers to be at peace when judgment falls on their nation, trusting God's perfect will and His promised deliverance.
teachings.text:
Now we're there in chapter 14 of Jeremiah and we see a continuation of what has become the pattern over the past few chapters, that Jeremiah is beseeching the Lord for mercy for his people while the Lord preaches through Jeremiah to them about their sin. And especially the judgment that has come upon them.

As it goes, we see Jeremiah becoming more desperate in pleading the case for the children of Israel. And we see God has hardened His heart against them. He is promising that they shall die by famine and by sword and be carried away captive into a strange land. God's mind is set upon this judgment and His wrath is upon them.

In chapter 14, we see Jeremiah begging not to do this to the people who call themselves by his name, Who are his people. And God says don't even bother praying for them. They can't make burnt offerings or fast enough for Him to repent. Reprobate, silver shellman call them because the Lord has given up on them.

Again, the parallels to today are striking. And again, we should remind ourselves that in all times and places there have been Jeremiah's. And there have been people who have done wickedly and received the just wrath of God.

Part of the  reason for the book of Jeremiah and lamentations that follow is to help set us in the right frame of mind and understanding when tribulation comes to our nations. When the wickedness of our people leads us to destruction. That we can be at peace with it even as we preach hard against it. Hoping that our people turn back to the Lord.

Much like Job and understanding how God deals with us as individuals, Even we who are righteous in His name.

But also like Job. It is easy to empathize and feel the emotion as they go through their trials and tribulations. The frustration of it. But it's humbling to understand that God's will is not our will. And God's point of view is outside of time and perfect while we see through a glass darkly. Our faith should be bolstered by reading this because we know how it turned out in the end. And we know how Israel was delivered by Christ and the resurrection promised in the scriptures by a God who cannot lie. And so we should take comfort in that as the people who call ourselves by His name. As we await a better country.

teachings.title: Fearful and angry all the time? Get right with God
teachings.summary: A believer constantly fearful and wrathful needs to get right with God, since tribulation should work patience and bring peace through His word and prayer.
teachings.text:
I've said it before and perhaps not often enough, but if you believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and are walking the best you can in the spirit, and you still find yourself fearful and angry all the time, no love for others, snapping at them, constantly frustrated and wrathful... Then there's something wrong with your Christian walk. Is something you need to get right with God about.

We talk with Him, as we stay in his word and in prayer, and God uses us for his purpose, You should find your faith increasing and the peace that passes all understanding coming upon you. You should find yourself a lot less afraid of the things of this world. And you should find yourself having more patience and long suffering for others, especially as tribulation works in your life and you see God bringing you out of it.

Whatever is troubling you, He is there to help you.

*Persecutions, afflictions, which came unto me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra; what persecutions I endured: but out of them all the Lord delivered me. Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.*

...*And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.*

...*These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.*

So if you find yourself discouraged and afraid. Remember this. See comfort in books like Jeremiah and Job. Consider the sufferings of Paul and how, at the end, He had been abandoned by most of the people he had helped bring to Christ. But yet he was of good cheer.

*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us. For the earnest expectation of the creature waiteth for the manifestation of the sons of God.*

teachings.title: Not every calamity is judgment for sin
teachings.summary: Some things happen by time and chance or simply for God's glory, so believers should not read every misfortune as punishment but make peace with God's will and live to glorify Him.
teachings.text:
We don't figure out what's right and wrong from circumstances, we aren't called to be superstitious. God doesn't instruct us to place our faith in rituals or washings, ordinances and observations. He calls us to serve others and to study His word.

There are blessings and judgments and promises and curses, God's wrath revealed against the workers of iniquity, His mercy revealed by those who believe on Jesus and are saved.

**Matthew 5:44-45**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

The Bible tells us that sometimes circumstances happen for no other reason that God willed it. That we may not know His purpose and it isn't our place to question Him. (Read **Job** to see how God views our second guessing Him!)

But man has the gift of pattern recognition, and it is hard not to see that the fates that befall others must be in answer to their sin. Jesus rebuked the people doing this;

**Luke 13:1-5**
*There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And Jesus answering said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.*

Some things are just chance. Some times things happen, and we can't say why.

**Ecclesiastes 9:11**
*I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.*

We need to have peace with this. It isn't all about us. We aren't special boys. We may get reproved and chastened by God for our sin. We may receive unexpected blessings because we walk in the spirit and do the things of God with a meek heart. Loving others the way Christ loves us. Nations might be judged for their wickedness. But sometimes things happen that God may be glorified.

Keep that in mind, that the Christian life's entire purpose is to give all glory to God, and reveal His grace and mercy from Heaven, to help the lost. To heal the brokenhearted.

teachings.title: Aaron's grief and God's longsuffering
teachings.summary: God is merciful and patient when grief leaves our heart unable to do His will that day, as long as we do not curse God or backslide.
teachings.text:
After having kin remove the remains, Moses calls Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, and instructs them to do as the Lord commanded, to eat the sin offering, cooked by the same fire that killed their brothers, that came from the Lord. To eat it beside the altar, because this is a holy thing, designed to teach the congregation of the separation of holy from unholy. From clean and unclean.

But later, Moses sees their portion of the offering burnt without the camp. Likely in fear of divine retribution, Moses seeks out the sons to rebuke them, but Aaron says it was his own fault. That he couldn't bear to do it given the events of the day and the loss of his eldest two sons. Aaron admits the error, but appeals to the fact that it wouldn't have been done in the spirit of God's command had he gone along and ate it, and that it wouldn't have been acceptable given his state. This excuse is acceptable to Moses.

It is important to make this distinction, that while we must obey God's commands and seek to diligently follow what His word tells us is right, there are times where our heart isn't in it. Our spirit is low. And unlike those who seek to add their own works to the glory of God, kindling His wrath, the Lord is understanding of our own weakness and longsuffering in His mercy.

Aaron held his peace. He had accepted the judgment of God. But he was still grieved. He was on God's program but it was too bitter that day. Aaron resumed his duties following this, but it was too much to bear at the time.

God is merciful and loves us. He is understanding that sometimes the truth of His word is bitter to us, in the flesh. His judgments may seem harsh to us at the time, and we may need a little time to come to acceptance. We must not use that occasion to curse God or to backslide. But He is patient.

teachings.title: Brethren who hold up our arms
teachings.summary: As we leave sin, attacks and tribulation increase, but trusting God and letting fellow believers hold up our arms gives victory.
teachings.text:
*And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.*

Short chapter. Pretty straightforward.

But note, as the Israelites left Sin, they were beset with tribulation and attacked by Amalek. As saved Christians we too will see more people attack us, more tribulation, as we leave sin. As we straighten up our former lives.

As we seek to grow in God and walk after the Spirit, people will attack us. Even family and friends. And, like Moses raising the rod, we will be winning when we are trusting in God.

 But we may grow weary. Our arms may fall, and trouble may seem to be getting the better of us. But surrounding ourselves with fellow believers, the brethren who will help hold up our arms, and the rock that is Jesus Christ, to rest on, we will be victorious.

But we have this written in memorial and preached to our ears, that we will know God is at war with Amalek from generation to generation.

Jehovahnissi, because the Lord will have war with them, the unbelieving who seek to destroy His people.

teachings.title: Climbing out of the hole sin dug
teachings.summary: Being saved does not remove every consequence of past sin; God gives the rope and light to climb out, and chastens those who despise it and backslide.
teachings.text:
A lot of new Christians, and many not-so-new, will become frustrated and despair that when they got saved, and began "turning their life around," that they still had to endure the pain and hard work of getting up out of the hole their old man had dug for them with their sin.

But that hole was a grave. And in it was death. And God has given us the rope to climb out of it, and the light above to guide us from the darkness.

That while the worst consequences are mitigated, and miraculous opportunities to escape are granted them, there is still a process of shedding sin in their life. There is still lost opportunity and easier paths lost to them by their choices. There's still a price to pay in this world.

People sometimes can only see the walls of the hole they are in, and the light above seems small and distant. And the climb difficult, to where they take occasion to despise the rope they've been given. And they backslide.

Sometimes God shakes the rope to draw their attention and get them back focused on the light.

As we will see with the children of Israel, that sometimes we see falling back into sin, going back to servitude in Egypt, as easier than getting right with God. And God will remind us the foolishness of this. Harshly.

*My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord; neither be weary of his correction: For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth*

teachings.title: Let my people go worship
teachings.summary: God led with letting His people worship, so Christians must make sure any persecution they suffer is for Christ's name, not for being riotous or rendering evil for evil.
teachings.text:
Moses and Aaron go before the Pharaoh, and speak the words God had gave them; allow the Israelites a 3 day release from their labors that they may assemble to worship Him. (3 days without labor, works, just as we see during Christ's death, burial and resurrection). And as God said, Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he not only said no, but added to the people's labors, making them gather their own straw for brick, while keeping the same expectations for output. And the taskmasters over them tell the people that it is due to Moses and Aaron's plea that they be allowed free to go and worship God.

And the people turn to criticize Moses, who in turn goes before the Lord and asks why God has not instantly freed them, and instead made their situation worse.

As we have already seen, Moses is not the most stalwart man of faith, and the people, as we will continually see, are stiff-necked and impatient with the Lord.

But we are called to be faithful and long suffering. To understand that God's timing is perfect and ours is lacking. To take joy in being persecuted for His name.

This is an important factor that needs to be reinforced, especially today.

God didn't lead with freeing the nation of Israel from the Egyptians. He didn't begin with plagues and curses. He led with "let my people worship." From that point on, everything that happens to the Egyptians is due to their reaction to this plea. The persecution of His people will be for His name's sake. This has to be every Christians starting point. Regardless of how harshly we are treated, make it be for God's sake. For Jesus' name. Not because we are riotous. Not because we will render evil for evil. But because our oppressors despise the Lord.

teachings.title: A sweet savour of Christ
teachings.summary: We should not care how we look to the world, since to the perishing we are the savour of death, but our obedience is a sweet savour to God and all things work together for good.
teachings.text:
*And the officers of the children of Israel did see that they were in evil case, after it was said, Ye shall not minish ought from your bricks of your daily task. And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood in the way, as they came forth from Pharaoh: And they said unto them, The Lord look upon you, and judge; because ye have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of his servants, to put a sword in their hand to slay us.*

The elders of Israel, its failed human leaders, take to task Moses and Aaron who, having done what God told them to do, even saying what God told them to say.

Remember in **Exodus 4**:

*And Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel: And Aaron spake all the words which the Lord had spoken unto Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people. And the people believed: and when they heard that the Lord had visited the children of Israel, and that he had looked upon their affliction, then they bowed their heads and worshipped.*

God had told Moses that Pharaoh would not allow them to go to worship Him. Moses told Aaron all of what God told him, and Aaron *spake all the words.*

They knew it wasn't going to be as easy. But at the first sign of tribulation, the elders come against Moses and Aaron for preaching and doing God's word. And they say "*you have made our savour abhorred in the eyes of Pharaoh."* These leaders are more concerned with how they look to the world than to God. But look what Paul writes in **2 Corinthians 2:15-17**:

*For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not as many, which corrupt the word of God: but as of sincerity, but as of God, in the sight of God speak we in Christ.*

To the world, we stink like death, because we remind them that they are perishing, but our obedience to God in Christ is a sweet savour unto the Lord.

We shouldn't worry about what the world thinks of us, even if it means persecution. We need to remember that all things, not some things, not a few things, not only good things, but *ALL* things work together for good to them that love God.

teachings.title: The more they afflicted them, the more they grew
teachings.summary: Christians should welcome persecution and trials, because God uses them to grow His people and increase His harvest.
teachings.text:
*But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.*..

**2 Corinthians 4**
*8 We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;*

*9 Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;*

*10 Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body.*

*Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad...*

In the days of the Hebrews sojourn in Egypt, in the days of Jesus ministry on Earth, in the days of the early NT churches, persecution and being reviled led to the greatest gains for God. The more they were troubled and suffered, the more the people of God grew, and grew stronger.

We as Christians should welcome tribulation and temptation. Being tested of God, by Satan, who, like with Job, seeks to accuse us before the Lord. "*Have you considered my servant Job?"*

**1 Corinthians 10:13:**

*There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.*

We are given trials because God has considered us worthy to endure and by doing so, grow in faith. We as a people are given tribulation, so that in glorifying God and rejoicing, we can grow mighty as his people.

More come to faith, more are called to salvation, more are brought to look for the light we reflect from the love and holiness of God, in times of trouble. And so God's harvest is increased.

We shouldn't look to persecution as a negative thing, tribulations as a curse, but a blessing. It means God has given us a chance to give Him glory. To pass through the fiery furnace unburned. To be like Job, blessed that *the latter end of Job more than his beginning.*

I heard a sermon this past week where the message was delighting in tribulation that God may be saying to the accuser, "*Have you considered..."* about you.

*But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.*..

Rejoice and stand tall in the Lord the way these Hebrew midwives did, doing the right thing for God, that we may grow as a mighty nation, and God will make a house of you. Amen.

teachings.title: Run the Race Looking unto Jesus
teachings.summary: Believers must lay aside guilt, bitterness and the cares of this world to run the race, receiving God's chastening as a sign of His love.
teachings.text:
Amen!

The pure hard preaching of Hebrews is building to a crescendo. The case made for faith in Christ Jesus, without the works of the law or traditions of man, against the temptations to backslide the way of Judaizers, but towards full faith in a better testament, nearly complete.

The Spirit through the author, telling us the will of God and reminding the hearers of His word the excellency of His faithfulness in keeping the promises and bestowing the blessings on those who came before us.  Those just who lived by faith. The saints named from the patriarchs and prophets, and the unnamed Christians  who for their faith in the promise of Christ suffered mockery, pain and death:

...*others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection: And others had trial of cruel mockings and scourgings, yea, moreover of bonds and imprisonment: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented; (Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.*

Many who endured in faith towards God's word, not seeing the promises but in hope knowing they would be delivered by the Lord, faithful and true.

And so we, who carry burdens, the weight of guilt, of bitterness at correction, of the distractions and cares of this world, which can lead to envying of the unsaved and impatience with God, to sin, to the fornication of putting the pleasures of the flesh before the promise of our inheritance and the blessings to come, Paul encourages us to standfast in the faith.

We have a race to run. A crown incorruptible to receive. The yoke of dead works and guilt for sins forgiven slowing us in our course. We must shed these things, striving for the mark set before us.

And where we slip, where we stumble, know it is God's correction, rebuking those sons whom He loves. Bringing us reproach that we may turn from the sin or shed the burdens that slow us down. For our edification we must not despise the rod of correction given us by our Father, but take joy in that He loves us.

*Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. For consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.*

If we consider Jesus, who literally authored the word that our faith hangs on, and finished it by the work He did, the first fruits of the resurrection assuring us of His faithfulness, if we keep in mind the shame of the cross which He endured for our sin and to do the will of He who sent Him. Our struggles with sin and the weight we carry in this world is nothing.

Cast it off least we be castaway.

teachings.title: Suffering wrongfully, taking it patiently
teachings.summary: Following Christ's example, suffering patiently for doing well is acceptable to God, while bearing punishment for our own faults is only the bare minimum.
teachings.text:
1 Peter 2:18-25

*Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.*

*For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.*

*For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.*

*For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously: Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.*

*For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.*

Peter, aware of his own falling short, encourages us to understanding that to suffer for God with good conscience, taking it patiently as Jesus exemplified, we shall be found acceptable to God.

Peter makes a distinction here, that if we be punished for our own wrong doing and accept the punishment, we aren't doing anything to glory of. That's just expected. It's bare minimum.

But how often do we fail even this, and find ourselves facing true accusations or the consequences for our sin, and yet rail against our accusers or lash out at our punishment? This when we are guilty, let alone when we are innocent.

Peter says Christ's suffering, *when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously* even though Jesus was blameless. Without sin. And in His patience suffered for us, carrying ours.

Jesus is our example; *For ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls.*

teachings.title: Stablished and comforted in tribulation
teachings.summary: All Christians will meet persecution, and those without deep roots wither like the stony ground, so we stay in the word and prayer and take comfort in Christ's return.
teachings.text:
Continuing the topic at hand from Chapter 2 regarding the persecution and tribulations the church at had been reportedly going through, Paul says He, Timothy and Silas were concerned for them and their faith, that they in their troubles have been believing in vain, and turned from practicing the faith. Unable to wait any longer, they dispatched Timothy, and he returned with good news that they were just as strong and stedfast, unmoving, as ever.

Establish and comfort means to to strengthen, to edify and be a bulwark. In modern terms, comfort is seen as weakening. Coddling, but it's meaning in the Bible is to strengthen in tribulation. This is why the Holy Spirit is called the comforter by Jesus. The evangelists sought to be a comforting encouragement to the saints in Thessalonica, but their stedfast unmoving faith, he says, actually brought comfort to him.

He expounds on the idea that all Christians will see tribulations, and persecution for His name's sake. He reminds them of that, and is warning us against being discouraged.

Believers can be like the seed from Jesus' parable of the sower, that;

...*fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth: and forthwith they sprung up, because they had no deepness of earth: And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.*

Jesus explained;

...*he that received the seed into stony places, the same is he that heareth the word, and anon with joy receiveth it;*
*Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended.*

These are saved Christians, but who aren't firmly established. Who aren't stedfast. Who, having shallow roots and not grown deep enough in faith, are moved by troubles. Wilting and producing no fruit when the heat is turned up. This is why it is important for us to stay in the word, in prayer, and exercising our faith to the benefit of others, that our roots are strong and we be immovable, stedfast and not offended by the inevitable persecution and troubles that come our way.

But Paul's fears of this are assuaged by Timothy's report, the Thessalonians were engaged and their faith alive, despite the persecution by their countrymen for that faith.

Paul sends prayers of blessings and restates his fervent desire to come and visit them, and reiterates that they take hope in the returning of Jesus Christ and the gathering of believers unto Him. This is a point made at the end of chapter 1 and again in 2, now fleshed out even moreso in chapter 3;

*And the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we do toward you: To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.*

This hope, the thing that we are convinced of by the evidence of faith, should remain a comfort. That the Christ who saved us is returning, and in that day, our resurrection. The gathering of the elect, of all saints. In the worst of tribulation, even unto death, this blessed assurance of eternal life in Jesus name establishes us firmly, so that we may not be moved. A rock unmoving.

teachings.title: Tribulation for His name brings reward
teachings.summary: Those who forsake all and suffer tribulation for Christ's name will rule with Him, so believers should not seek to avoid the tribulation that brings reward in heaven.
teachings.text:
Finally we see peter, always ready to ask a question whether it is prudent or not, asking what reward then do they have, having already renounced all of their worldly goods to follow Him, having already received an inheritance in the kingdom of God for their faith that He was the Christ. And Jesus responds that they will have seats of judgment, over the 12 tribes of Israel in his kingdom when it comes. And that all who forsake or lose anything in his name, suffering tribulation, or division from family and friends, being maligned for our faith, persecuted, led to martyrdom even, that these will rule over the Kingdom of Heaven with him.

So many Christians today seek to avoid tribulation, when it's that very tribulation that gives us rewards in heaven.
