They do fruitless works of self-righteousness, a thinking that by them they will achieve salvation. Meanwhile it is the meek, and the humble who inherit the kingdom of heaven, the poor in spirit. And they who suffering tribulation, keep the faith holding on knowing that a reward not made of hands, but of God, awaits them.

teachings.title: The God of all comfort in tribulation
teachings.summary: God comforts us in our troubles so we can comfort others, and sealed with the earnest of the Spirit we can count even tribulation as giving glory to God.
teachings.text:
Paul writes his second epistle to the church at Corinth, approximately a year following the first. As we know from Acts, his plan to go to them was derailed, slightly and instead, elders of the church went to him as he traveled, and so he writes with some apology in his greeting. That the troubles he came to in his travels that prevented him from going to them, were actually blessings.

He acknowledges the truth of the Gospel is in them, as it is in him, and that of the hope of eternal life we also receive the comfort of God in the Holy Spirit.

The message, that in our tribulations and troubles, we have comfort, given by God's grace, and in that comfort, the ability to give the same comfort with grace an understanding to others in need. Thus, his tribulation and that which the churches experience are a gift, that gives us consolation and salvation from trouble, that we may provide the same to others.

He reminds them that if our faith in God is to the hope of the resurrection and eternal life, then there's nothing we can't place on God to deliver for us.

This is the goal of a Christian life, to see not only riches and good fortune as blessings, but troubles and tribulations even unto death, as giving glory to God.

The gift of prayer for others is a gift that is repaid with thanks in prayer, towards God, "Who hath also sealed us, and given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts."

We are sealed unto the day of judgment, and the ernest, or the down payment on the promise of eternal life, is the Spirit living within our hearts. And so with this knowledge, the testimony of our faith living within us, we can trust in God. His promises are 'yea, yea.'

It's a beautiful introduction and sober reminder that in God, all things are possible and we needn't be troubled by anything in this world, because in Christ we have already overcome it.

teachings.title: Neither hath this man sinned
teachings.summary: Infirmities and hardship are not always the fruit of sin but may be for God's glory, as with Job, so we should not be respecters of persons.
teachings.text:
John 9 is an interesting chapter, where almost all the action and dialogue happens away from Jesus and with the Pharisees in the synagogue.

The opening exchange with the disciples asking Jesus who's sin caused the man's blindness and Jesus' reply that it was neither, but a chance to glorify God, His works made manifest in him is an awesome and often overlooked doctrine. While the wages of sin is death, and we see health issues and poor fortune may at times be the result of sin, infirmities from birth, or even hardship in life are not necessarily the fruit of sin, but to God's glory. Very similar to the lesson of Job.

As fleshly humans, we sinfully become respecters of persons, and assume based on status, fortune and health that we are "better or worse than," and see God's hand in punishing and rewarding, relative to ourselves, when it's not how we should look at others. Sometimes covetous. Sometimes prideful. When we should look at every opportunity as to how we can glorify God, win souls and edify believers. It's hard.

teachings.title: God is our refuge and strength
teachings.summary: The scriptures' promises of God as refuge and fortress are real expressions of faith forged in trouble, kept by the gift of His Son and witnessed by the Spirit of adoption.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 46:1**
*God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.*

**Psalm 91:2**
*I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.*

**Proverbs 18:10**
*The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.*

**Psalm 18:2**
*The Lord is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.*

**Psalm 121:7**
*The Lord shall preserve thee from all evil: he shall preserve thy soul.*

**Deuteronomy 31:6**
*Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the Lord thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.*

**2 Thessalonians 3:3**
*But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.*

**Isaiah 41:10**
*Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness*.

**Psalm 34:17**
*The righteous cry, and the Lord heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles.*

**Nahum 1:7**
*The Lord is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.*

These are not platitudes or empty promises. These are real and observable and heartfelt understandings and expressions of faith, forged in troubled times.

God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son to keep this promise. God commanded His love towards us that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

We know, by the testifying of the Holy Spirit inside of us, that Spirit of adoption, that we are the Father's and His children are protected.

teachings.title: God is our refuge and strength
teachings.summary: Throughout the Bible God is our refuge, and the gospel itself is His promise of protection and life kept in Christ.
teachings.text:
The opening verse of **Psalm 46** is a wonderful text on the faithfulness and protection of God. It has been preached on an untold number of times, been made a life-verse for scores of people, been pinned to walls, stuck on refrigerators, is a prominent part of hundreds of thousands of devotionals, verse of the days, and used in countless facebook memes.

What a comfort for believers in trouble these words have been and continue to be.

Again and again, the Bible tells us that God is our refuge and strength. Our buckler, our fortress, our shield and strong tower. The promise of protection extended to the children of God is found throughout the word, and ultimately the entire Bible is a promise of deliverance from a holy and merciful God.

The Gospel itself is the promise of protection and life, from God to all who come to Him. And the promise is kept in the Son, the Lord Christ Jesus.

He is our rock. He is our strong foundation. He is the gathering hen, protecting her chicks under her wing. He is the Good Shepherd, watching over the flock, His love for His sheep so deep, that He laid down His life for us.

God is very present, always with us, desiring to be our Comfort, to be involved in our lives, and our shelter in the time of storm.

And in any Christian life, given enough time, this is proven to us again and again.

teachings.title: I trusted in thee: let the wicked be ashamed
teachings.summary: In grief and isolation we trust the Lord, who saves us despite our sin, while the wicked who deny Him will be silenced in unquenchable fire.
teachings.text:
Continuing in **Psalm 31**, picking up in verse 9. The gladness and rejoicing in God's mercy and crying out to Him in the earlier stanzas, brings us the heart of the matter, the trouble in David's life, and reflected in our own struggles.

He says I am in trouble, consumed with grief and physically and spiritually affected by the tribulation in his life. This is something everyone alive can relate to. Anyone alive long enough to be broken hearted. Betrayed. Lied about and persecuted.

*For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.*

When we are going through it, it can feel as though all we ever have known is grief. We can feel all alone, when not only our enemies abandon us, but our neighbors and friends won't even look at us. So miserable and alone.

We may feel forgotten as a dead man, out of sight out of mind. Truly miserable. Feeling as though the whole world has conspired against us. Having no where to turn or anyone to trust.

*But I trusted in thee, O LORD: I said, Thou art my God.* What a beautiful reminder that we have a friend in Jesus. We have a Lord who is trustworthy and Who cares. Whose face shines on us, and saves us. Not because of how good we are, but despite our sin. For His mercies' sake. Because He so loved us.

We plead, *Let me not be ashamed, O LORD; for I have called upon thee*, and we know that God, Who cannot lie, has promised us deliverance. L*et the wicked be ashamed, and let them be silent in the grave.* We will sing His praise forever, while they are tormented by unquenchable fire, where the worm dieth not.

**Isaiah 66:24**
*And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh.*

**Mark 9:47–49**
*And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out: it is better for thee to enter into the kingdom of God with one eye, than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire: Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched. For every one shall be salted with fire, and every sacrifice shall be salted with salt.*

All those that have denied the truth of God shall be silenced. They shall be made to be ashamed. Let the wicked be ashamed, but we have trusted the Lord.

*Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous.*

teachings.title: The LORD preserveth the faithful
teachings.summary: Like Elijah we may feel alone, but God has reserved His own and will preserve the faithful from the wicked.
teachings.text:
*Oh how great is thy goodness, which thou hast laid up for them that fear thee; which thou hast wrought for them that trust in thee before the sons of men!*

The culmination of the Psalm is a tribute to the richness of God's mercy and fidelity in times of trouble, and the sure destruction of those that hate Him.

God shall hide those that trust in Him from the wrath to come. Shield us from the wicked, guard us from the strife of their tongues, their slander and railing will come to nothing.

Bless the Lord for His marvelous kindness. For the protection He has granted those that trust in Him. Even when we feel alone and desperate. Even the great prophet, Elijah, fresh from a great work for God, and a spiritual highpoint, felt alone and in his haste thought he was cut off from before God's eyes.

**Romans 11:3–4**
*Lord, they have killed thy prophets, and digged down thine altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal*.

We might have moments of doubt, when God's perfect timing isn't lining up with our own. When we think we cannot go on. That there are Jezebels and her men after us. That we are all alone. But God has reserved His own. We will be preserved. We can comfort ourselves and others with this truth.

*O love the LORD, all ye his saints: for the LORD preserveth the faithful, and plentifully rewardeth the proud doer. Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart, all ye that hope in the LORD.*

Amen*.*

teachings.title: The Lord is my shepherd in this life
teachings.summary: Psalm 23's promises are not automatic for all the dead but belong to believers by faith in Jesus the Good Shepherd, who supplies every need and gives peace and comfort in this life's valleys.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 23** is perhaps the second most famous passage of scripture, behind **John 3:16**, and like it, contains the gospel promise, the good news of the Lord towards believers.

The world knows the Psalm because it has become the standard go to, in fiction and in real life, recited at funerals by priests and reverends, in every religion that claims the name of Christ. Sadly, for most, the departed have no idea that the promises are not automatic, and aren't achieved by their works, their character or how "good" they are. They are by faith in the Good Shepherd, alone.

Of course, Jesus is that shepherd.

**John 10:11**
*I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep*.

He gave His life that we may be forgiven, and rose again that we may have eternal life. He did this for those that follow Him, and who have been entrusted to Him by the Father. Believers are His flock.

And because He is our shepherd, we shall not want.

What an amazing promise, which God Who cannot lie has given us. We shall not want. He provides all things:

**Philippians 4:19**
*But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.*

Not riches as this world judges, necessarily, but all our needs are met by Him by Christ Jesus.

**2 Peter 1:3**
*According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue.*

You may feel financially burdened, or pressed by health concerns. You might be struggling in your faith, to live by trust in God to deliver. But ultimately, the truth is that all we need, everything that pertains to life and godliness, is given freely, that we may have life and more abundantly in His name.

The green pastures and still waters are generally equated to Heaven in the way the world uses **Psalm 23**, and certainly, what little we know of Paradise is the peace of being in the presence of the Lord. But this stillness is a promise of this life, for a believer.

**Philippians 4:7**
*And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.*

Our burdens aren't removed, but the yoke of carrying them is made light by His grace. Because in the end, whatever we are going through will be for our good.

**Romans 8:28**
*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.*

We are renewed in Him, and regenerated by the Spirit in faith, our soul restored. We are led in His ways, and shown the truth from His word, for His name's sake. In Jesus we are made whole, and by His power revealed in us, by His word, we are shown the deeper things of God.

*Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.*

This allegory is considered death itself by the secular world, but note the imagery of a shadow. The Bible says a shadow is not the very image of the things that cast it.

We may be in a low point in our lives, a valley, and maybe even feel the shadow of death on our flesh as we endure this season in our lives, but the strength to fear no evil, to glory in our tribulation, comes from knowing the good Shepherd is with us. His rod and staff, our comfort.

The rod of correction, the staff that guides us as we go astray. His protection, our safety. Knowing He laid down His life for us. That He will seek and save His lost sheep, and bring us home by His power.

What the unsaved world uses as a false comfort in death should be a comfort in this life for saved believers.

The table He has set for us, the bounty of His blessings, the deliverance from those who seek to destroy us, that they may know we fear the Lord, and glorify Him, is in this life. In the presence of our enemies.

Yes, there is the idea of a feast set for us in the end times prophecy, a wedding feast for the Bridegroom. Served by Christ Jesus:

teachings.title: Goodness and mercy shall follow me now
teachings.summary: Though it points to the marriage feast, Psalm 23 mainly speaks of the peace and provision believers have now, along with eternal life.
teachings.text:
**Isaiah 25:6**
*And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.*

**Luke 12:37**
*Blessed are those servants, whom the lord when he cometh shall find watching: verily I say unto you, that he shall gird himself, and make them to sit down to meat, and will come forth and serve them.*

...but the primary application in **Psalm 23** is the peace found in this life. At this time. Our cup runneth over with His grace, even now. The table has been set in Heaven, but the bounty we are given starts the moment you call upon His name in faith.

The final verse places this context firmly in the "now" of the believer:

*Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.*

Goodness and mercy follow us, today. We can rest assured that He has delivered us, and be blessed in this life, knowing we have eternity with Him in the next.

We shall fear no evil, because we have eternal life and shall never perish. We will dwell in the house of the Lord forever, so rejoice even in perils and trials. Rest in the green pastures by the still waters. We have a good Shepherd Who loves us. Amen

teachings.title: Our fathers trusted in thee and were delivered
teachings.summary: God's faithfulness to the fathers, written for our learning, assures our deliverance even when we feel abandoned.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 22** continues from its powerful open, to convey the desperation that Jesus' flesh must have felt in that moment, which is felt by everyone of us at times in our life. Certainly, it was David's own state of mind when the Spirit led him to compose it.

That we cry out to God, and feel like He is far from us. That He doesn't hear. That He may have abandoned us to our plight.

But there is always the hope of faith, and trust in the holy God, Who has kept His promises and delivers those who trust in Him.

The promises made to the fathers, kept. He heard the cries in Egypt, and brought them out of the land. He heard their cries during the time in the wilderness. He delivered their children to the promised land. He heard them in the days of judges, where their own sin brought them low, sending men to raise them up and bring them out of evil.

Those that trusted Him were not confounded.

**Hebrews 12:1**
*Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us*

We know that God is good, and cannot lie. And so our deliverance is assured, even when our flesh is weak and we feel abandoned.

The almighty God's consistent faithfulness in keeping his word to those he foreknew, gives us confidence and strength. These things were written for our admonition. That we may know Him as a rewarder of those who diligently seek Him.

**Romans 15:4**
*For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.*

We are given that knowledge of the past that we might have the surety of the future.

teachings.title: Some trust in chariots, but we in the name of the LORD
teachings.summary: Trusting the Lord rather than wealth or strength makes us sure of deliverance in every battle because we first trusted Him for eternal security.
teachings.text:
*Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.*

This verse is often quoted, and has inspired generations of believers. But in practice it can be difficult. We often seek reassurance from our material, wealth and position.

David, writing this. Psalm with dual purpose (at least), the prophetic imagery of Christ Jesus and the surety of his salvation, but also as an intercessional prayer before a battle against a well-armed and equipped foe.

David's showing us that it is better to trust in the Lord than all the horses and chariots in the world. That in our battles, even if we are seemingly overmatched by our enemy, we are still victorious in God.

What a comfort. What a blessing. That we can stand fast, and be sure of our deliverance. That we can trust in the Lord in all things, because we've first trusted in Him, our eternal security.

When we are weak we are made strong. God uses us to confound the wise. We have already overcome in Christ. And we should rejoice in our salvation.

teachings.title: If the foundations be destroyed
teachings.summary: Believers need not fear or flee from the wicked, even in the Tribulation, because Christ is risen and is the sure foundation, while the wicked will drink the cup of God's wrath.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 11** is a short song addressing a doubtful disputation of an unknown interlocer, someone who may say our faith in the Lord is insufficient to save us from our enemies.

Our trust is in the Lord. We have no need to fear. To flee. Especially in the end times this Psalm's dual-fulfillment of prophecy, portends.

I think of all the fairweather Christians who spend their days in fear, prepping to flee to the mountains in the Tribulation. Who plan to flee as a bird to their mountain.

The wicked seek to shoot their arrows at the hearts of the upright, even now. In the Tribulation, they won't need to do it privily, but will openly seek the lives of the children of God.

David asks, rhetorically, *If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?*

If the Lord isn't true to save us, if the foundation of our faith is destroyed, we would of all men be most miserable.

**1 Corinthians 15:13–17**
*But if there be no resurrection of the dead, then is Christ not risen: And if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God; because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ: whom he raised not up, if so be that the dead rise not. For if the dead rise not, then is not Christ raised: And if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain; ye are yet in your sins.*

Because there is no other foundation upon which we may trust;

**1 Corinthians 3:11**
*For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.*

Knowing this sure foundation, and knowing He is risen, we can place our trust in Him.

We know with certainty the Lord is in His holy Temple, the Lord is on His throne. We know He is the omnipotent judge of men.

He tries, or tests the righteous to increase our faith. He hates the wicked and the violent, and shall rain down His wrath upon them. This is the portion of their cup. This is a promise of God.

**Revelation 14:10–11**
*The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.*

But the righteous are before the face of the Lord, always.

teachings.title: Two are better than one
teachings.summary: Solomon shows the world's oppressed and oppressors have no comforter, but believers have the Comforter and Christ who bears their load and gives rest.
teachings.text:
The chapter opens with an observation of the oppressed and the oppressors. Solomon the Preacher says he began to consider oppression, and noted that despite the tears of the oppressed, they have no comforter. They cry alone in their tribulation. But, he also takes notice that the oppressors, despite their power, also lack a comforter.

That, since all of life is travail, and the endless work, vanity, there is no difference between the oppressed and their oppressor, fundamentally. They lack a comforter, someone to share the burden and lift them up against the vexation of spirit, of being ground down by the cycle of life.

Yet, Jesus has promised us all a Comforter.

**John 14:16-20** 
*And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever; Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you. I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you. Yet a little while, and the world seeth me no more; but ye see me: because I live, ye shall live also. At that day ye shall know that I am in my Father, and ye in me, and I in you.*

With Christ, we are never alone. We are never without God. We have this blessed assurance and indwelling of the Spirit, as temples of God.

But, the Preacher is preaching to the world, who do not know the good news, and in a time when the Holy Spirit only came upon man for a brief time to do the works of God through them.

And so, to the world he declared it is better for the dead than the living, because it is better to be free from the lonely vexation of the troubles and tribulations of the world.

Where the right works of one man lead his neighbor to covet the results of a man's travail, but it is all vanity.

The fool foldeth his hands, the same sluggard analogy from Solomon's Proverbs, and in their laziness, they eat their own flesh, they destroy themselves. Better to have little and have peace, than much from vain works and the vexation of spirit that comes with it.

This is not prescriptive, but descriptive. If the works of life are almost meaningless, except the brief moments of joy from the fruit of the labor, then why strive for more?

Solomon is building a case of hope, by challenging the futility of the worldly outlook of life.

He turns his attention to the empty works of toiling without an heir. Neither son nor brother. *For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.*

He proclaims the truth that two, working together, are better than one. They have more reward for their labor, lifting one another up as they go. Again, as we with the Comforter can attest, those in Christ never walk alone.

But for man, striving to toil under the Sun, it is better to do so with others. Solomon compares it to the difference between sleeping alone and cold in the night, and the warmth of shared body heat by being with another. Alone, we feel the biting cold, but together, somehow, our combined body heat is a comfort to the cold.

That together, if in a one on one fight, you may lose, with another, you win. If two attack, you can withstand them. If three, by two you can hold them off for a while.

The importance of having another to share the load is the point, and again this points to Jesus, Who not only helps shoulder the load, but bears it all on Himself. He carries us in Him, and gives us rest. And nothing shall overcome us.

**Isaiah 46:4**
*And even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you*

**Matthew 11:28**
*Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.*

teachings.title: The name of the Lord is a strong tower
teachings.summary: The righteous run into the name of the Lord and are safe, while the rich trust in their wealth as a high wall in their own conceit, which will be their downfall.
teachings.text:
Solomon then compares the words of a talebearer, or a gossip, to wounds. Deep cuts, to the innermost parts of the belly, wounds that fester there.

*He also that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster*.

These negative qualities, talebearing, lazy and a waster, someone who casually destroys the store, wasting food, or clean water...character traits we should guard against.

Then, as in most chapters of Proverbs, we find another gospel message;

*The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.*

This promise of deliverance by Christ is contrasted with what the rich man puts his trust in;

*The rich man's wealth is his strong city, and as an high wall in his own conceit.*

We must choose the honor of humility, seeking that strong tower of the Lord, rather than the haughty pride of the man who places his trust in the walls he has built for himself.

The application here is spiritual, although there's a practical matter behind it. Even if you're afforded the ability to surround yourself in a walled city, remember that your refuge is in the Lord.

But a man may spiritually believe they are immune to destruction, because of their wealth, because of the high walls they have placed around their sin, their trust in themselves and their works, and that conceit will be their downfall. Humble yourself to recognize, God is the only shelter you need.

teachings.title: The enemies' tactics against Nehemiah
teachings.summary: Nehemiah's enemies used threats, lies, flattery and betrayal, as the world does against believers, and the answer is to keep doing the Lord's work without fear.
teachings.text:
Nehemiah bears the end of the construction of the walls and gates and his enemies still seek to destroy him.

When they realize they cannot lure him out, they threaten to defame him that the authorities of the King of Persia will come and destroy him for rebellion. But he isn't tricked and he calls them out on their lies.

Then they seek to have him violate the sanctity of the temple in fear, sinning. Again, his faith is in the Lord and he refuses and continues the work to completion.

Then the nobles of Jerusalem, who are in league with Tobiah, and intermarrying with his family begin to tell Nehemiah what a good guy he is, and to convince Nehemiah while at the same time Tobiah is sending him threatening messages.

These are common tactics of the enemies of God. Truck, threaten, betray, seek to have you sin, tell lies about you, flatter you, and get those with influence in your world to turn on you, while they try and get the powers that be against you.

The Jews did it to Christ. He says, because they hated Him first, they'll do the same to us.

But Nehemiah continues to the end, doing what God commands. Faithful that it will work out for good.

He doesn't waste time exchanging railing for railing or fighting with them. He just does the work of the Lord.

This is all we can do. Trust God. Don't fear.

**Isaiah 41:10**
*Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.*

teachings.title: Egypt a broken reed
teachings.summary: Like Judah leaning on Egypt, believers must not lean on the world's supports, which God may remove so we depend on Him alone.
teachings.text:
Continuing the prophecies against the nations in proximity to Judah, we have in **Ezekiel 29** two against the kingdom of Egypt.

The first prophecy, in the 10th year, 10th month, 12th day (around 587 BC), was given during the siege of Jerusalem, before its fall in 586 BC (the 11th year by the prophets reckoning, which uses the reign of King Zedekiah as a starting point). This is when Egypt was still a potential player in the region, promising aid to Judah against Babylon.

God's anger at the Jews who turned to Egypt for help is found throughout the prophets, particularly Jeremiah.

Because Egypt represents the old, unsaved life of Christians, under bondage to sin, we can draw an application here to not turn to the world for help when we are in trouble, but to turn only the the Lord.

God says Egypt is like a staff of a reed, the hollow and weak grass that grows by a river. Especially the Nile. That Israel leaned on for support, but it buckles immediately and they bruise their shoulder and put them in the ground.

We should look at the world's solutions to our problems the same way. Weak and insufficient, knocking us on our butts when we rely on them.

The second prophecy is made 16 years later, (571 BC) and comes after Nebuchadnezzar’s prolonged siege of Tyre (circa 585–572 BC), which was costly and yielded little reward, as Tyre’s island fortress was difficult to conquer, although it destroyed Tyre's power. This later prophecy clarifies that Egypt would be given to Nebuchadnezzar as a “wage” for his efforts against Tyre.

The word of God said that Egypt would be scattered and taken into captivity for 40 years, (echoing the 40 years Israel spent in the wilderness) and when it gathered again, it would never be as powerful. This way, when Cyrus gives the go-ahead to the Jews to rebuild Jerusalem, there's no temptation to lean again on Egypt.

In your Christian walk, this sort of thing may happen, where the supports you have among friends, family, alcohol and drugs, old habits and lifestyles, even hobbies and activities, may be taken from you for a season, long enough to not be available to you for support or shelter, and if they ever come back around, their weakness is obvious. You cannot count on them. It is the Lord only we can depend on. Amen.

teachings.title: Trusting in Egypt is death
teachings.summary: Egypt pictures the world and our old life of bondage, and God's children must not turn back to it for help in tribulation.
teachings.text:
The prophetic warning to Judah, that when their time of tribulation came, the captivity to Babylon, not to flee to or trust in Egypt to save them, was fulfilled in Jeremiah's day.

He also warned them, referring back to the prophets, beginning with Isaiah. God, knowing what they would do, warns against it. And you know those in Jerusalem who believed the word of God did not flee, and be destroyed in the way.

The dual fulfillment here is also clear, the Holy One of Israel, the Lord Christ Jesus at His second coming and the wrath that pours out from His lips, the fire of Tophet, a name for Hell, is lit from the brimstone from His mouth, that kindles it.

Egypt is a representation of the world, our pre-Christian life of sin, under the yoke of the law, slaves to sin. As the Bible says again and again of the Israelites being led by Moses, that in their freedom they would long to return to the bondage of Egypt out of fear or inconvenience.

**Exodus 13:17**
*And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt*.

This is written for our admonition, that we who are His children don't turn again to the world and to sin when we face tribulation. That trusting in Egypt is death.

We all come out of Egypt. We all are baptized in the crossing, and sojourn in the wilderness, awaiting the promised land.

The promise of paradise on the other side is the hope of our faith. Without that hope, we fear and faint. Relying on the world to save us is folly, we should suffer gladly that the Lord delivers us.

The wicked will be punished. The Lord will fight for us, and destroy those that trouble us, and has a place prepared for them, deep and large, the pile is fire and much wood. The breath of the Lord is like a stream of brimstone. Amen

teachings.title: Crying unto the Lord from the depths
teachings.summary: Jonah's prayer, like David's Psalms, shows the believer in distress turning to the Lord with thanksgiving, knowing He hears and delivers even from the depths.
teachings.text:
**Jonah 2** in light of the Gospels, shows the reluctant prophet as a type of Jesus, the willing Son. The three days and nights in Hell being the sign Jesus said would be ignored by the Jews, even as the Gentiles of Nineveh received the word.

The prayer of Jonah echos many lines of the Psalms, where David cries out for salvation, calling upon the name of the Lord for relief.

**Psalm 69:1-3**
*Save me, O God; For the waters are come in unto my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me. I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: Mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.*

The form and function of the prayer, like the Psalms, show us how we should be in times of distress and tribulation. Constantly turning to the Lord to be our salvation, remembering His loving kindness. Thanksgiving in the face of adversity. Knowing God will not forsake you or fail you.

When we are at the end of our rope, our soul fainting, we can know He hears us. Even at the depths of the sea. Even were we in Hell itself. The Lord hears and delivers us. Amen.

teachings.title: God is not in the wind
teachings.summary: Ephraim fed on the wind as the world chases winds of doctrine and clouds without water, but God is in the still small voice in our spirit, keeps a remnant, and has work for us.
teachings.text:
*Ephraim feedeth on the wind*; Israel are placing their hopes against desolation and famine on Egypt and Assyria, not God.

This reminds me of Jesus, speaking to Nicodemus in **John 3** about how the Spirit seems to man;  *The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth*. And also in **2 Peter 2**, *clouds that are carried with a tempest*, *clouds without water,* in **Jude 1:12.** Carried *to and fro by winds of doctrine* from **Ephesians 4:14**.

But, God is not in the wind;

**1 Kings 19:11-14**
*And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the Lord. And, behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the Lord; but the Lord was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the Lord was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the Lord was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice. And it was so, when Elijah heard it, that he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entering in of the cave. And, behold, there came a voice unto him, and said, What doest thou here, Elijah? And he said, I have been very jealous for the Lord God of hosts: because the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.*

But even then, the Lord had reserved unto Him 7,000 men who had not bowed the knee to Baal, and God had work for Elijah to do.

Even as the world looks for answers in the wind, and seeks truth from clouds without water, and is carried about by the winds of doctrines, and even as they forsake His covenant in Christ and kill His prophets and seek our lives, yet we know God is not in the wind. He isn't in the tempest. The Lord our God is in the still small voice, heard in our spirit, and He has work for us to do.

teachings.title: Jehoshaphat's assembly of prayer and praise
teachings.summary: Because Judah had been brought back to God by revival, they could fast, pray and sing in tribulation and see God deliver them, as a believer walking in the Spirit can boldly ask God for deliverance.
teachings.text:
The final entry in the Chronicles of Jehosaphat's reign. We see here that the godly king's faith, and his efforts in leading revival among the people brings them to be able to call upon the Lord in adversity, and know He would not forsake them, but deliver them as He has promised.

While not perfect in all his ways, Jehosaphat consistently sought the Lord. Even when he yoked with Ahab in their failed battle with Syria, he insisted the wicked king inquire of the prophet Micaiah.

And so, when the armies of Ammon and Moab and Mt Seir assemble against Jerusalem and her king, Jehosaphat calls the people together. A called out assembly in fast, and prayer, and singing songs in praise of God. Calling on Him to remember His promise, showing they have faith in His word.

Because of all the legwork, soul-winning, hard preaching, keeping the word of the Lord, Judah is right with God and able to do this in good conscience.

They weren't perfect. There were high places still in the land. Not all their hearts were continuously with the Lord.

But, generally the people were faithful and believed. And so in time of tribulation, with the armies gathered as the sand of the sea, the Lord confounded them, turning them on one another until they were all dead.

Just as He will defeat the armies of Satan after the millennium. While we stand firm and sing praises to His name.

A Christian who walks in the Spirit, who first seeks the things of God, praying and reading the Bible, going to church. Putting the profit of others above their own, can boldly go before God to ask for deliverance, knowing He is faithful and true.

teachings.title: Asa sought the physicians, not the Lord
teachings.summary: Doctors and allies may be God's tools, but we must go to God first and trust Him, since His withdrawal of protection from the consequences of our sin is His sorest chastening.
teachings.text:
As mentioned in yesterday's study, Asa over time turns his trust from the Lord to himself. To his treasure (that the Lord provided), to men, physicians, and ceased from going to God first. Especially after swearing oaths and vows to serve God with his whole heart.

Now, when we are beset by enemies, we may find allies and win friends to help defeat them, but first go to God and He will bring these things into being.

If we are sick, there's nothing wrong with using doctors, medicines, etc...but first go to God in prayer. Place your trust in Him, not men or things. Those men and those things may be the tools with which God heals you or delivers you, but it is God's mighty hand that we need.

*For the eyes of the Lord run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him. Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.*

God's greatest means of punishment, the most brutal cord of scourging, is His withdrawal of protection against our suffering the consequences of our own sin.

Thus we should seek His tender mercies everyday. Thanking Him for not judging us in His hot displeasure. Humbling ourselves before the Lord.

teachings.title: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord
teachings.summary: Like Habakkuk facing desolation, believers in great tribulation or personal trouble can rest and rejoice in the God of their salvation, who remembers mercy in wrath.
teachings.text:
The final chapter of the prophet Habakkuk is a song, written in the Spirit, apparently upon a stringed instrument for the chief singer to sing. A *Shigionoth* may be the name of that instrument. It is also thought to be a style of prayerful song, but the Bible defines itself, and the closing verse indicates it was an instrument used to write this prayerful song.

Habakkuk writes of his fear of the word of the Lord he received, of the judgment against wicked Judah by the hands of the Chaldeans, and the judgment that will come upon Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon after they are used by the Lord for this purpose.

The prophet asks that in the midst of the years, during this time, that in His wrath God remembers His mercy.

He recounts that God came up from the South, from Tenant and mount Paran, in the wilderness where the children of Israel came, up towards the promised land. That His glory filled the heavens and the earth full of His praise, His brightness as the light. This is the Lord that was with them, the fathers in the wilderness who entered into the promised land as His people, and He their God.

*He had horns coming out of His hand*...horns being leaders in the Bible, God sets up captains and kings over people and takes them down. He sent pestilence and fire before them, and drove the nations of Canaanites asunder. The mountains scattered and hills did bow, the great nations that were there before Israel.

He asks, *Was the Lord displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?*

We know that His wrath was against the people and their abominations. But the prophet is poetically saying that even the mountains and rivers were affected by the fury of God's wrath. Even the oceans deep, and the sun and moon stood still;

Joshua 10:13
*And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed, Until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. Is not this written in the book of Jasher? So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day.*

The prophet sings that God marched through the land in indignation and thresh the heathen in anger, while being the salvation and deliverer for His children, and *even for salvation with thine anointed*, a mention of Christ to whom all prophets gave witness.

It is important to remember this, that the promise of salvation in His anointed, (Christ means anointed one, Messiah) was the faith of the Israelites in the wilderness, and of the saved throughout the Old Testament.

Habakkuk describes how the Lord destroyed the rulers and delivered the land to them in violence and wrath. And then he says his lips quivered and he trembled and rottenness entered his bones knowing that the same wrathful vengeance was coming against Judah in his day. That the Lord would be doing to them what He did to the people before them.

*Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.*

Even so, in this time of tribulation and even in the desolation he describes, Habakkuk says he will find joy in the God of his salvation. He will rest in the day if trouble.

This is a great illustration of the way we, as saved believers, should approach the Great Tribulation should it come in our day, or even individual troubles we may have. In the midst of days, the Lord remembers His mercy. We have rest. We find joy in the God of our salvation.

We would do well to remember this.

*The Lord God is my strength*. Amen.

teachings.title: Seven thousand who have not bowed
teachings.summary: After great triumphs believers may feel despair and alone as Elijah did, but God always has a remnant and still has use for us.
teachings.text:
And so, Elijah the prophet of Israel, fresh from being used by God unto mighty works, flees from the wrath of Jezebel, wife of King Ahab.

Elijah shut up the heavens from rain, causing three and a half years of famine by the word of the Lord. He was fed by ravens, and by meal and oil that never ran out or spoiled. He called upon the Lord and saw the widow's son raised from the dead.

By faith, Elijah returned to Israel and confronted the king and the 450 prophets of Baal, and by the word of the Lord called down fire from Heaven to show the children of Israel the power of the living God. They slew the prophets of Baal. And by the word of the Lord, rains came and returned to the land.

During the challenge to the prophets of Baal, Elijah claimed to them that he alone still followed the Lord and against the 450. He met Obadiah, who kept his faith secret for fear of the king and hid prophets of God in a cave, an act of cowardice compared to mighty Elijah.

And yet, Elijah fled. And went beyond Judah, to Horeb. Mount Sinai, where God appeared before Moses with the Law, and lived in a cave.

The triumph that should have led to revival brought depression and fear in the prophet. He wished to end his life.

He says: *I have been very jealous for the Lord God of hosts: for the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.*

Again, saying he was alone in his zeal for the Lord as he had boasted to the priests of Baalim. But the Lord corrects him here; *Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him.*

In our Christian life, even after seeing the power of God on us and having great triumphs of faith, it isn't unusual to feel a sense of letdown afterwards. To have doubts. To feel alone. But the Lord works in more than us. And we are never alone. There is always a righteous remnant, and despair isn't an option even in the face of tribulation. God has use for us yet.

teachings.title: Be of good courage and play the men
teachings.summary: Christian men should not cower or force outcomes in fear but behave valiantly, obey God and trust Him to give the victory.
teachings.text:
*Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God: and the Lord do that which seemeth him good.*

*Be of good courage, and let us behave ourselves valiantly for our people, and for the cities of our God: and let the Lord do that which is good in his sight.*

This encouraging message of faith given by Joab before what could have been a haplessly outnumbered battle, with his forces split and surrounded, should be a mantra for Christians, especially Christian men.

Too often today, professing Christian men come off as afraid, behave with no honor or duty to their people, and do not trust in the Lord to do what He sees as right.

We see it daily, especially among the "conservatives," and even the more right-wing. Men, who seeing the odds and thinking that it's "so over," that the "West has fallen," either cower in fear, retreat from the world to hide, or take up blindly reactionary causes to "do something!" and force outcomes without any faith in the Lord to provide victory.

But the Bible tells us again and again to have no fear. In the life of David we see that he behaved like a man, valiantly. Having the morality of God to guide him and following His word. Trusting in the Lord to deliver him and his people. And in his leadership, King David's faith and attitude trickled down to his captains, and from them to their men. And eventually to all Israel, rising up to put an end to the threats facing them, when God delivered victory against their enemies.

That's the secret to winning. To win souls and obey God, live righteously and trust in Him when the battle comes.

teachings.title: The battle is the Lord's
teachings.summary: David's victory over Goliath was the Lord's, teaching that our deliverance and victories come not by our own works or weapons but by God.
teachings.text:
The familiar story of David and Goliath. How a shepherd boy slew the giant with one smooth stone. It is one of the most well known stories in the world, a feat everyone has heard of and a byword for overcoming impossible odds. But the world doesn't see the lesson; that it wasn't David who overcame Goliath, but the Lord. David's faith wasn't in himself, or his weapon of choice, but the power of God to deliver him.

*The Lord that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine*...

...*Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied. This day will the Lord deliver thee into mine hand; and I will smite thee, and take thine head from thee; and I will give the carcases of the host of the Philistines this day unto the fowls of the air, and to the wild beasts of the earth; that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. And all this assembly shall know that the Lord saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord's, and he will give you into our hands.*

It is not by works we have done. It is not by our own cunningly made devices and armor. Our sword or our strength, but His.

And all the earth knows there is a God in Israel, that our God is true and delivered David. That God doesn't save by sword and spear but He wins the battle and delivers salvation into our hands.

The parallel with the spiritual things of God, the Christian life of trusting in the Lord. Our victories are His, that the assembly may know that it is the Lord that delivers us. The battle is His.

teachings.title: The battle is already won
teachings.summary: Trials are not for proving ourselves alone; growing faith means leaning more on God, who has already given us the victory.
teachings.text:
Sometimes Christians get the mistaken idea that tribulations and temptations and attacks by adversaries are sent by God to test our faith, to prove ourselves worthy of His love. And so they will try to go it alone to show God how strong they are.

This is a mistake.

**Romans 5:6-8**
*For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.*

God loves us so much, despite our weakness, that He sent His only begotten Son. That Jesus so loves us, He died for us while we were yet sinners.

Yes, God wishes us to grow in faith, and shapes us by our experiences to be better vessels for His purpose. But increased faith doesn't mean relying more and more upon yourself, but rather leaning more and more upon Him to deliver us.

Like Gideon, we may have fears and doubts, and require signs. But the Lord knows and understands, and will surely provide us with a way out. He will provide us with a Phurah, to go with us into the breach. Like Barak needed Deborah with him.

He will ask for our trust, and to stand firm and do as He commands, but the battles are already won by Him. The Lord delivered us already. We have overcome. This is how He increases our faith. How He helps our unbelief.

God uses the weak. He uses foolish things to confound the wise. No one would think that 300 men blowing trumpets and smashing pots and shouting could rout tens of thousands. What a foolish plan! But they had already been delivered into Gideon's hands by the Lord.

Just as the Israelites were delivered from Egypt. Just as Jericho fell. Just as Jael the housewife had victory over Sisera. Just as the giants were destroyed and the land was delivered, and 33 Kings were toppled in a single campaign.

Just as death and Hell have been conquered. By the mighty hand of God.

When we are tempted, tested and tried, remember this, God has already given us victory. We just have to obey His word, be watchful and ready to act on the opportunities He will provide.

**1 Corinthians 10:13**
*There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.*

teachings.title: The Lord goeth with you to fight
teachings.summary: As God promised to fight Israel's battles against greater armies, the God who delivered us from sin and hell will deliver us in life's smaller battles.
teachings.text:
**Deuteronomy 20** has some practical advice for the Hebrews, who are headed into the land promised as an inheritance by God, especially in their devising armies to go to war.

The Lord tells first reassures them that if the odds appear stacked against them to have no fear. That He fights with them and is with them. That their faith in victory is faith in His promise to deliver. So much so, that rather than draft every available man to make the battle more even, to send home those that have other obligations. Even those who are faint of heart and afraid. That the Israelites won't need them to win.

This is of course a reassuring message as believers. That any battle we face in life, that we can remember it is the same God who fights for us. The same God who delivered us from Egypt, and the bondage of sin under the law; The wages of death and Hell. And if He can deliver us from that, He can deliver us from the small battles we have here in this life.

**Romans 8:18**
*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.*

And again, it is a picture of God doing the work to deliver us, He does it all. Even against seemingly impossible odds. As Jesus says, *With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.*

*When thou goest out to battle against thine enemies, and seest horses, and chariots, and a people more than thou, be not afraid of them: for the Lord thy God is with thee, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt. Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble...For the Lord your God is he that goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.*

Amen!

teachings.title: Christ pleads our cause; fear not
teachings.summary: As Jeremiah cried out of the dungeon, believers in their lowest points call on the Lord, who says fear not, pleads our cause and assures our deliverance.
teachings.text:
*I called upon thy name, O Lord, out of the low dungeon. Thou hast heard my voice: hide not thine ear at my breathing, at my cry.*

*Thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee: thou saidst, Fear not. O Lord, thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul; thou hast redeemed my life.*

*O Lord, thou hast seen my wrong: judge thou my cause.*

Remember, Jeremiah was literally thrown in a pit of mire, the depths of a prison, for the cause of his faith. And here, again echoing Christ's decent onto Hell for our transgressions, a burnt offering for our sin, we in our lowest points as believers likewise call out for our deliverance. And the Lord says; *Fear not*.

Jesus pleads our case, redeems our soul in His blood, by His sacrifice. Drawing near to us. And so we ask Him to judge our cause. That His will be done.

When you have believed, there is no calamity or trials that the Lord will not help us overcome. We simply must ask and He will plead our cause and judge those who are against us, and deliverance is assured. Nothing will come between us and His mercies. So be not afraid.

Amen

teachings.title: If thou hast run with the footmen
teachings.summary: Believers should not envy the prospering wicked or complain over small troubles, but grow faith that does not fear, knowing God delivers and vengeance is His.
teachings.text:
In this morning's reading of **Jeremiah 12**, we find the profit and the Lord in a conversation. Jeremiah is lamenting that the wicked seems to prosper while the righteous are afflicted. And God reminds him that vengeance is His. The wicked get what they deserve. This is a theme throughout the Bible, and it is one of the things that should bring us peace as believers. That God is our deliverer. Regardless of the tribulations or afflictions in this world, already overcome through Christ. And so we shouldn't be discouraged or downhearted or even envying the wicked, cuz their punishment will be far worse than any blessing they appear to have in this life.

But God also points out that many times a discouraged or resentful spirit in a man comes more from a lack of faith and complaint about the unimportant cares of this world.

**Romans 8:18**
*For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.*

**2 Timothy 3:12**
*Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.*

**Philippians 4:12-13**
*I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.*

As many daily devotionals out there will tell you, God tells us 365 times in the Bible to not be afraid. He promises us that he will deliver us from all our difficulties in this world, even if it's only after being redeemed into the next. That eternity without tears is ours for our faith in His Son.

God promises that the wicked will pay. And his wrath revealed from heaven shows us this.

And just as God promised, Israel in the covenant made with them in the wilderness, and that he keeps hammering through Jeremiah here, If we walk with Him, we will be blessed beyond measure.

And yet, so many times we fall victim to fear. To resentment. To frustration that the wicked aren't suffering while we seem beset from all sides.

*If thou hast run with the footmen, and they have wearied thee, then how canst thou contend with horses? and if in the land of peace, wherein thou trustedst, they wearied thee, then how wilt thou do in the swelling of Jordan?*

God asks, if we complain about such little things, if we aren't able to deal with the small challenges life brings, how can we hope to deal with the great tribulations that may come?

We see so many Christians here in America, where we are still free to worship Jesus and share His gospel without interference or genuine persecution, who constantly complain about how hard it is. How "persecuted" they feel. They have a social media account suspended and they act like it's being cast into the fiery furnace.

If we, in the land of peace wherein we've trusted, can't handle things, what will we do when the river floods? When all of the evils of this world come crashing down on us?

God wants us to have faith, not just in Christ for our redemption, but then building on that faith, such that the cares of this world become nothing, knowing that God who loves us is with us. For if He be with us, who can stand against us?

And when God, who promises us all things that we ask for, according to His will, delivers, when our needs be met, over and over again. When we turn to Him and He blesses us, our faith should grow. The more you walk in the spirit, the more you see how consistently God pays off His promises to us. And so we should never fear.

teachings.title: All things work together for good
teachings.summary: God who spared not His Son will give us all we need, so all things, even tribulation, work for good and we should not worry over money, politics or persecution.
teachings.text:
*And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us? He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?*

And so, being justified by faith, being given the promise of eternal life, having our spirit quickened, being sealed by the earnest expectation of the day of redemption by the Spirit, testifying within us, we are promised that in our cries, in our gutteral utterances and incomprehensible groanings as we travail in this life, awaiting another, as the flesh frustrates our will to do that which we should, God promises that His Spirit as intercessor, and that all we ask for or need He will know and provide, as it conforms to His will.

The Father who gave us His only begotten Son as a sacrifice for our sin, that we may be adopted heirs into His Kingdom, will not be slack concerning His promises to us. He will give us all we need. And all is good, even tribulation, because we love God and have faith in His righteousness.

If we walk in the spirit, we shouldn't worry about the things of this world. Money, politics, persecution, the various temptations that Satan and his children leave for us as snares. These are temporary. Material. Worldly.

Instead we should focus on the eternal. The will of the Father. Servants to the Gospel. The just will live by faith.

teachings.title: Immanuel, God with us
teachings.summary: The merciful God who knows His people by name is present with them always, as promised throughout the Old and New Testaments.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 1:23**
*Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel” (which means, God with us)*

The power of God being with us, to be our God and we His people, to show the world His grace and mercy by our being a separate nation. A holy people. And He will be there in our midst that all may know His glory. This is found throughout the Bible. Old Testament and New.

It is the assurance of having the Lord God Creator with us. Even as we are a stiff-necked people. He scatters our enemies before us as He leads us to the promised land.

God knows us by name and loves us in His mercy.

**Jeremiah 1:5**
*Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.*

**John 10:14-15**
*I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.*

**John 10:3**
*To him the porter openeth; and the sheep hear his voice: and he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out.*

**Psalms 91:14**
*Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name*

A merciful God, who knows your name and who is present with you, always.

**2 Samuel 7:23**
*And what one nation in the earth is like thy people, even like Israel, whom God went to redeem for a people to himself, and to make him a name, and to do for you great things and terrible, for thy land, before thy people, which thou redeemedst to thee from Egypt, from the nations and their gods?*

**Isaiah 41:10**
*Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.*

**Deuteronomy 31:6**
*Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.*

**Matthew 28:20**
*Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.*

Amen

teachings.title: The hosts of angels about Jacob
teachings.summary: God sets His angels over the saved to protect and guide them, yet like Jacob we still scheme in our own strength when our real battle is with God and our vow to serve Him.
teachings.text:
Jacob, having left behind Laban and having his wives and children, cattle and riches with him, now faces the thing that drove him from his father's land to begin with; Esau's murderous vow against him for deceiving Isaac and taking the blessing from his older brother. (Jacob means deceiver/grabber).

He can't go back, having just escaped and made covenant with his father-in-law. But in pressing forward, he may lose everything. His life has been blessed by God, despite his schemes and his dishonesty. Despite taking advantage of Esau's hunger to take the inheritance. Despite his fooling his father. Despite his haggling with and ultimately tricking Laban.

Now, his vow to God at Bethel is come due. He was taken care of and blessed by God, now it's time he fully commit and serve the Lord, even if it means dying there at the hands of his brother.

Quite a spiritual crisis.

As they make their way, Jacob looks and sees the hosts of heaven, angels all about him.

**2 Kings 6:17**
*And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.*

**Psalm 91:11-12**
*For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone.*

**Hebrews 1:14**
*Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?*

Anyone who has been a saved Christian for any meaningful  length of time will testify to the fact that the Lord places angels over us, protecting us, often from ourselves. Providing a path out of sin and temptation. Guarding us from the worst of the consequences of our foolish actions or placing us directly in the path of them, if it brings us closer to God.

We are given understanding to just how protected we are that God may have the glory. It's often at a time where our own sin is wrestling with us to try and fix things ourselves, as a reminder that God is prepared to if we had but the faith to let him.

Jacob now facing this moment of crisis. Messengers to his brother return saying Esau is following with 400 men. It looks fire. This is the crisis he feared, one he built for himself. And though God allowed him to see the hosts of angels about him, yet he begins to plot and scheme, as is his way.

He splits the troop in two. He concocts a bribe and a script for all to say, hoping it would stave off his brother. He tells them to say to Esau that he is here as his servant. That these gifts are a sign of respect. He's hoping on his own devices to save all he has, but his real battle is with the God who has blessed him, and his vow to serve Him.

teachings.title: I believe God, that it shall be as told me
teachings.summary: Paul's shipwreck pictures the Christian life in stormy times, kept by God toward His purpose and called to be a steadfast anchor and example to others.
teachings.text:
I won't even try breaking down the narrative of this chapter, as Luke writing in the spirit paints a thrilling picture of the perilous voyage of the centurions taking Paul to Rome.

Paul's visitation by a messenger of God, promise to save the crew and passengers. The fasting of the believers among them, the breaking of bread and the casting off of the wheat to the sea. The centurion saving the prisoners from death by his soldiers, for Paul's sake.  Their eventual wreck, and being castaway on the shore.

God has purpose for us, and in that use we see a hedge of protection that still allows for the free will of others to make bad decisions and ignore sound advice. Not a hair harmed as God carries us towards His purpose, in His time and manner.

All of this journey serves as an allegory for the Christian life, in tumultuous times. That we should be as an anchor, steadfast in our faith. Trusting in God's promises. An example for others. Giving sound advice in a sea of storms to those seeking safety of the shore. Offering them salvation of the spirit, even as it was told unto you.

So, *be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me.* Amen

teachings.title: They that wait on thee shall not be ashamed
teachings.summary: Psalm 25 models trusting prayer: lifting our souls to God, confessing sin that may bring chastening, and waiting on Him, never ashamed.
teachings.text:
The powerful prayer of **Psalm 25** is a model for all that trust in the Lord, and a doctrinally-rich reminder of why we should. That we who wait on the Lord will not be ashamed.

Verse after verse, the psalmist has us call upon the name of the Lord, as we read or sing through the Psalm. And verse after verse we are reminded of His mercy and faithfulness.

We lift up our souls, every fiber of our being, unto the Lord, and He delivers us from our enemies. Those that trust in Him are never ashamed, but those that reject His truth are.

We are shown His ways, taught His statutes, walk His paths, and we are preserved in this life, and established in the next.

The meek and his seed shall inherit the earth, and in meekness we humbly admit our sins and ask for God's mercy, to forget them. His lovingkindness is established from old, and the God of our salvation keeps us by His power, unto redemption. What an amazing God we have. How can we not serve Him in truth. Truth of Who He is, who we are, and the reconciliation we have with and in Him, despite our sins.

The Lord teaches sinners like us in His way, and the meek share this truth with the world.

His secret, His covenant, is shown to us. And that good news is spread abroad by those that fear Him, that others may know the mystery of the gospel, and be saved.

*Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.*

**Proverbs 3:6**
*In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.*

**Galatians 5:16**
*This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh*.

Looking to Jesus the author and finisher of our salvation, we are lifted from the nets, the snares of sin set for us by the wicked. Walking in the Spirit. Acknowledging the ways of the Lord.

With importunity and persistent prayer, we remind Him of the goodness He has shown us, and ourselves of the grace we have found in Him. Our troubles become lighter, as His yoke is easy. He brings us out of our distress.

The pain we feel, He understands. The affliction that besets us is often due to sin. Seeking forgiveness, because our troubles may be chastening by a loving Father. Getting right so we may be lifted up by Him. Delivered, because we put our trust in Him. Never ashamed, because His word is true. Waiting on the day of the Lord, and the redemption of all Israel. All His people who trusted in the Lord. Amen

teachings.title: Waiting on God's perfect timing
teachings.summary: Impatient waiting in trials should give way to remembering God's bountiful dealing and salvation, since patience in waiting on the Lord renews strength and builds godliness.
teachings.text:
Psalm 13 beautifully captures a very real feeling of the Christian life, the impatient waiting for God's perfect timing, turning into an acknowledgement that He has dealt bountifully with us.

It can be easy to slip into despair when facing trials. It can be easy for us as humans, weak in the flesh, to see the enemy seemingly triumph. To pray and wait upon the Lord, but feel like He may have forgotten you in regards to your trouble.

We've discussed the idea that even as martyred saints in Heaven, this impatient call for the Lord to hurry and fulfill His judgment, occurs. How much more can this take hold in our finite flesh?

As Peter reminds us;

**2 Peter 3:8–9**
*But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance*.

God calls upon His faithful to wait. And in that waiting, there is promise as well.

**Isaiah 40:31**
*But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.*

In our patience, God gives us added strength. It is part of a ladder of virtue in the Christian life, elevating us to godliness.

**2 Peter 1:5–8**
*And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity. For if these things be in you, and abound, they make you that ye shall neither be barren nor unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.*

In the end, our prayers for God to act, and reminders that He has promised to tend to our welfare, and bring us peace from our enemies must inevitably lead to our recognition of His mercies and blessings. Of His salvation.

Because, as we call out to Him, it is impossible to not remember the very reason we are trusting in Him, beginning with eternal life granted through Jesus. And with the heavenly perspective of God's grace, it is incredibly difficult to continue in complaint. *Because he hath dealt bountifully with* us. We've already received more than we could ever deserve.

teachings.title: Job's longing for death and Paul's strait
teachings.summary: Job's longing for death was trust in God's final summons, like Paul's desire to depart, but believers should redeem the time and leave the timing to God.
teachings.text:
Job’s longing for death is not despair but a plea for release into the only comfort he still trusts: God’s final summons. “Let Him not spare me” is not suicidal rage; it is the confidence that his end is with the Holy One. Even here, in the furnace, Job confesses the rock beneath his feet, Christ Jesus, his strength and hope. The rebuke of Eliphaz therefore wounds doubly: it is not merely unfeeling; it is faithless. To kick a brother when he is down is to forsake the fear of God.

The presence of faith in Job's response to this unspeakable tragedy has been consistent. The vain theology of karma that Eliphaz offers is predicated on the idea that Job deserves what's happened, while Job in his heart knows his trust is in the Holy One, his Redeemer.

It is similar to the struggle Paul felt, as he wrote to the Philippians from his bondage in Rome, potential death by execution, certain.

**Philippians 1:20-24** 
*According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour: yet what I shall choose I wot not. For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better: Nevertheless to abide in the flesh is more needful for you.*

It can be tempting in trials for a believer to long to be called home. But, better to redeem the time while we are here. God's perfect timing is His, not ours.

teachings.title: Ezra's refused escort: faith or tempting God
teachings.summary: Ezra trusted God without an armed escort, but there is a fine line between faith and tempting God, and help offered may be God's own means.
teachings.text:
Here in **Ezra 8**, he recounts the genealogy of those that came down to Jerusalem from Babylon, carrying the treasure for the house of God.

It lists the key patriarchs of the lead families, each with significant roles. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, secured a priestly covenant through zeal. Ithamar, Aaron’s son, upheld temple duties. David, the iconic king, represents royal and messianic legacy. Shechaniah, meaning "YHWH dwells," ties to divine presence. Parosh ("flea") led a resilient clan. Pahath-moab ("ruler of Moab") suggests foreign integration. Joab ("YHWH is father") was a chief warrior for David's mighty men. Along with the others, each are given a pedigree to note the continuity of things, going back to Jacob, Moses and Aaron, and David.

The integration of Moabites and others after the captivity, into the ranks of "Jews," is something that is often contested, and will come into play here in **Ezra 9** and **10**, but it's interesting.
